The bulb over the table had gone brown with age. It gave off just enough light to see Detective Vale take my license out of my wallet and just little enough for him to pretend he couldn't read it.

“Occupation?” he said.

“You hired me once.”

“That was my wife.”

“She paid, too.”

Behind me, Detective Dugan picked up the city phone book. A second later I was on my side, still in the chair, looking at a piece of gum stuck under the table.

“No bruises,” Dugan said. He sounded like a salesman repeating a guarantee he hadn't read.

The pain took its time. First I wanted air. Then I got some and wished I hadn't. The room stank of cheap tobacco, that damp, sour stuff that used to cling to my father's coat. For a crazy second I wanted to put my face in the collar of that coat. Then Dugan hauled me upright and I was forty-three again, with nobody coming to get me.

Vale laid my license on the table. “Where's Ruth Bell?”

“Last time I saw her, she was standing over her husband. One of you boys ought to remember. You were there.”

Dugan's cigarette made a little tick when he tapped it against the radiator. Downstairs a typewriter stopped. I wondered how much the girl at the keys could hear, and what it cost her to start typing again.

Vale pulled his chair closer. “Eddie Bell was a thief.”

“Then you should've arrested him.”

“He reached inside his jacket.”

“For his spectacles. Ruth showed me. Still in the case, with a bullet through it.”

Dugan hefted the book again. Vale looked at him, and he set it down. For the first time all night I felt a little better. Dugan was scared of Vale. Vale was scared of a woman who took in hems for thirty cents a skirt.

“You think that widow gives a damn about you?” Vale asked.

“No.”

“Then why lie here and take this for her?”

I worked my tongue around a loose tooth. “I wasn't lying here. Your partner tipped me over.”

Downstairs the typewriter started up. Vale waited until the keys were going good and steady before he spoke.

“What does she want?”

There it was. Not *where is she* this time.

“She wants his watch back,” I said.

Both men looked at Dugan's wrist. He'd been wearing the damn thing for three days. Hadn't even taken off the little green thread Ruth had wound around the broken keeper.

Dugan covered it with his cuff.

I shut my eyes. Everything hurt, but I could still see that thread. In a whole precinct full of cops, somebody had finally bothered to look at the evidence.

Mara had put up the title to her garage. For most of the week that had meant a piece of paper in a bookie’s safe. Now, waiting under the viaduct with her engine shaking the fillings in her back teeth, she pictured her father’s blue coveralls still hanging on the peg by the door.

The girl between the cars dropped her scarf.

For eight seconds there was nothing in the world but the white sedan beside her. Its rear tire spun and caught, flinging grit against Mara’s door. Burning rubber came in through the vents, sharp over the sweet stink of gasoline. At the first bend the cars drew so close she could see a little crescent of bare skin between the other driver’s glove and his sleeve. Then he blinked, backed off, and she was ahead.

She laughed. Couldn’t help it. The speed was glorious.

At the far end of the freight yard, the sedan’s headlights dipped behind her. He was braking for the turn. Mara gave it one more heartbeat and put her foot down.

The pedal went to the floor as softly as if she’d stepped into snow.

Her foot came up. Went down. For one stupid instant she thought she’d missed the pedal. She actually looked.

In the mirror, the sedan was already turning. Beyond it she caught a glimpse of the starting line, and remembered the man who’d been crouched beside her car while the bookie counted her money. *Dropped my lighter*, he’d said. She’d moved aside to let him up. Now her brakes were gone, and all she could think was that she’d said *sorry* to him.

The floodlit concrete barrier filled the windshield. There was time to see a weed growing out of a joint in it. There was time to say “No” quite clearly.

The left front corner struck first. The wheel tore out of her hands. Her car climbed the barrier in a bright sheet of sparks, rolled onto its roof, and slid through the finish banner upside down, dragging both light stands with it. One burst against the pavement. The other kept turning on its bent mast, sweeping the yard with slow white circles.

When the car stopped, Mara hung in her belt with glass in her hair. Gasoline dripped somewhere close. The smell that had thrilled her at the line made her gag now.

Shoes crunched toward her. Someone knelt and reached through the space where her window had been. A black glove, a little crescent of bare wrist.

“Look at me,” the other driver said. His hand was shaking. “Mara. Look at me.”

She did. Behind him, every time the light came round, she could see the finish banner stirring on the ground.

The caption under the photograph read ADRIAN VALE, 54. The number was new to him. The photograph was not.

Mercer sat at the little desk under the hotel television, his rifle resting on a folded bath towel. He worked a gray smear from the side of the receiver with a square of cotton. The finish had worn thin where the bolt handle met the stock. It had been that way for years. The pale crescent was as familiar to him as the chip in his front tooth and interested him about as much.

“Vale was pronounced dead at County General at four forty this afternoon.”

Mercer put down the cotton and made a note of the time. The announcement satisfied the last condition of his agreement. It was not necessary to watch the rest, but the room was paid for until morning and he disliked looking for something to watch more than he disliked the news.

They interviewed a woman outside the hospital. She was holding a brown paper bag against her chest. A reporter asked whether her father had known she was there.

“I brought him his glasses,” she said.

The reporter waited. Evidently the woman had intended to say something else, because she kept her mouth open for a moment. Then she folded the top of the bag down one more turn.

Mercer drew the cotton along the rifle’s comb. He liked hotel desks of this vintage: real veneer, enough depth for his forearms. In newer places there was often only a shelf.

People in his profession sometimes spoke of taking a life as though a life were an object now in their possession. He had never understood the expression. He had acquired nothing of Vale’s. Somewhere a house still contained the man’s shoes. His daughter had his glasses. What Mercer had was a contractual obligation, now discharged. For a few seconds that afternoon the distinction had required his full attention. It no longer did.

At the bottom of his invoice was a box marked *Expenses*. He entered the room rate and the parking charge. He left out dinner; he would have eaten somewhere regardless. The client had never questioned an expense, which Mercer considered no reason to submit a questionable one.

On television they were showing Vale at a school ceremony, failing to cut a ribbon with an enormous pair of scissors. A child came forward with a small pair that worked. Vale laughed. It was good footage. Even with the sound off, you knew exactly what had happened.

Mercer put the rifle away. He sent the invoice and hung the towel over the bathroom rail, gray mark inward. Then he called the front desk to ask when breakfast started.

“Six thirty,” the clerk said. “Will you need a wake-up call?”

He considered it. There was nowhere he had to be.

“No,” he said. “Thank you.”

Then she lifted her lantern and saw that the black line around her boot was moving.

The first bite felt like a burr caught in her sock. She bent to pull it free. By the time her fingers reached it, there were a dozen more, and when she straightened, her fingertips came away wearing little black caps. She shook her hand. Most of them fell. Two hung on, their mandibles working, their bodies swinging with the motion of her wrist.

She ran for the ladder. Behind her, the lantern rolled in a slow circle, sending her shadow racing ahead of her and then bringing it back.

Hundreds of bites ought to have blurred into one pain. They didn’t. She felt each new one distinctly: the pinch, the little wrench as the insect leaned back, the hot sting it left behind. Her skin seemed to be drawing tighter and tighter around her. She slapped her neck and felt shells break against her palm. In the instant of relief that followed, she heard them eating.

It was a small, industrious sound. Close to her ear, she could make out the paired clicks of a single set of mandibles. Farther down, along her shoulders and back, the clicks ran together into a soft, steady rasp. It reminded her so exactly of her father sanding a chair leg that for one bewildered second she could smell his workshop.

Her hand closed around the bottom rung. She pulled. The wood held; her fingers didn’t. She slid back to the floor.

Overhead, beyond the open hatch, someone called her name.

“Here,” she tried to shout. It came out quietly, but the footsteps stopped. A face appeared in the square of daylight. For a moment they looked straight at each other.

Then the lantern went out. In the dark, with nothing left to see, the sound of the mandibles was enormous.

The first thing June recognized was the squeak of Ollie’s shoe.

It made the same small, embarrassing sound it used to make on the gym floor. For half a second she was so glad to hear it that she called his name.

Then she got her flashlight under the basement stairs. Ollie lay on his back with one foot wedged against a support post. Each time June shifted her weight on the step above him, the post flexed and the rubber sole squeaked.

She got off the stairs.

His shirt was still tucked in on one side. On the other it had ridden up over a great purple swelling. His belly had split beneath it, and a wet, gray-pink fold of intestine rested in the crook of his elbow. There was plaster dust on it. June kept wanting to brush the dust away. Of all the things she couldn’t fix, that one seemed possible.

Something ticked in the laundry sink.

Mara sat on the floor beneath it, her head tipped back as if she were at a salon. The tap leaked onto her forehead. Water ran through her eyebrow, into the hollow where her left eye had been, and over her cheek in a thin pink track. Her other eye was closed. She had little silver stars painted on her lids; June had held the mirror for her that afternoon. One star remained, perfect down to its five tiny points.

June turned the tap until the ticking stopped.

In the quiet she heard somebody breathing.

“Ben?”

Behind the furnace, a hand lay palm up in a stripe of light. She knew the half-moon scar at the base of the thumb. She dropped to her knees and caught the hand in hers. It was warm.

“I’m here,” she said.

She pulled. The hand came easily, and with it six inches of forearm. The pale ends of two bones knocked against the furnace housing. Heat from the pilot light had kept his fingers warm.

June set the hand down. She took care not to let it knock again.

The breathing went on. It had a whistle at the end of it, familiar and almost funny. She’d broken her nose playing softball in eighth grade. It was her. She closed her mouth and the basement went quiet enough to hear a car pass on the road outside, tires hissing on wet pavement. Somebody out there had the heater on. Somebody was going home.

Her light found Ben at last. He was folded into the narrow space behind the furnace, his face turned to the wall. All she could see was the back of his head and the white tag sticking out of his collar.

She wanted her mother with a force that made her teeth hurt.

Above her, the basement door swung shut. The latch caught.

June switched off the flashlight. For a moment there was nothing, not even the sound of her breath.

Then Ollie’s shoe squeaked.

The first thing Jonas learned about the woman he had killed was that her left shoe pinched.

He had expected something solemn. Instead he was hurrying across Platform Six with a blister, annoyed at his sister for being right about the shoes. There was a pear in his coat pocket. He put a hand around it to keep it from bumping his hip, and felt the little give in its flesh where it had already bruised.

Then the glass doors shut. Beyond them, in the control booth, stood Jonas.

The memory ended there on the first day. The prison nurse peeled the contacts from his temples and asked him to rate his distress from one to ten.

“Her name was Ada,” he said.

“I know,” the nurse said. “One to ten, please.”

On the second day the memory ran four seconds longer. Smoke came rolling down the escalator ceiling, almost beautiful in the way it followed every curve. Ada pressed the yellow call button. She was not frightened yet. There was a man in the booth. He had seen her.

Jonas had spent the two years since the station fire remembering that look through the glass. He had remembered it as an accusation. It was worse to learn it had been relief.

On the third day he felt her understand.

It happened without words. The man in the booth took his hand off the release and backed away, and her body knew before her mind did. Her knees loosened. Her mouth filled with spit. She pressed the call button again with absurd politeness, one short press, as though a long one might annoy him.

Behind her, somebody began knocking on the glass. Ada wanted her sister. Not to say goodbye. She wanted her sister to come and get her, an impossible, childish want so complete that for a moment she was eight years old in the municipal baths, unable to find the bottom, waiting for a familiar hand to catch her under the arms.

No hand came.

There was still air near the floor. She lay down. The pear rolled out of her pocket and stopped against the door. On the far side, Jonas was gone. The terror was not a scream inside her. It was the effort of drawing one more breath while knowing what would be in it. It was having to do it anyway.

When the chair let him go, Jonas lay on the infirmary tiles with his fingers hooked beneath the gap in the door. The nurse sat beside him until he could uncurl them.

For six months the state made him go back. On Fridays an evaluator asked what he would do differently. Open the doors, he said at first. Later he said he would refuse the order to seal the platform. Both answers earned him green marks on his file.

In the seventh month Ada’s sister came to see him. She had petitioned eleven times to have the recordings withdrawn. Jonas had not known anyone could object.

“They say it’s working,” she said.

He looked at her hands. He knew those hands, one thumb crooked from a childhood break. He had no right to know them.

“Was she thinking of me?”

The prison had given him workshops on remorse, on restitution, on speaking without asking to be forgiven. None had prepared him to possess something this woman needed.

“Yes,” he said. “She wanted you there.”

Her face creased. “I’d have come.”

“I know.”

It was the wrong thing to say. He knew because he had been inside a place where Ada had kept that certainty safe all her life. He wished he could give it back without keeping a copy.

At his next evaluation, the screen asked him to describe the most distressing part of the experience. For months he had written about the last breath. This time he wrote about the first morning, the shoe and the pear, the private irritation with a sister who was usually right.

*She didn’t leave those things to me,* he wrote.

The evaluator read his answer twice. “You understand that declining further treatment will affect your release date?”

“Yes.”

She turned the screen so he could sign. It was the first time anyone in the building had asked permission before doing something to a memory.

He signed. The door stayed shut.

The dragging stopped. From beneath the bed skirt she could see the worn heel of one boot. Her ribs gave a sudden, miserable hitch. For one awful second she couldn't tell if the small sound she'd heard had come from her throat or from the floor.

She kept thinking he had stopped. Then it would come free with a knock she felt all the way down to her back teeth.

A tear ran across the bridge of her nose and into her other eye. She wanted to wipe it away, but the bed was so low that even lifting her elbow would brush the sagging springs. She let it sting. Crying quietly had seemed possible until her nose closed up. Now she had to open her mouth to breathe, and every breath out wanted to be a sob.

The dragging stopped. From beneath the bed skirt she could see the worn heel of one boot. Her ribs gave a sudden, miserable hitch. For one awful second she couldn't tell if the small sound she'd heard had come from her throat or from the floor.

The heel lifted. The axe scraped on.

“Your eye,” Vale said, “or I hurt your daughter.”

June looked at her father, waiting for him to explain. She was six. If a stranger said something frightening, you looked at Dad, and Dad told you what the stranger had really meant.

He wanted, absurdly, to ask which eye. As if this were an appointment he could get through by listening carefully and following instructions. Then June said, “Dad?” and what little shelter there was in that thought fell away.

“I’m here,” he said.

“Can we go?”

That undid him. He had spent all morning hurrying her out of the house. Shoes, June. Coat, June. Come on, sweetheart, we have to go. He would have given anything to stand in that hallway again while she took ten whole minutes to do up one red button.

Vale pushed the knife across the table.

His arm felt heavy until he lifted it; then it felt horribly light, liable to jerk sideways and knock the knife to the floor. His fingertips brushed the wooden handle. There was a nick in it, a tiny raised lip that caught against the pad of his thumb. He could feel that one small thing with extraordinary clarity. The rest of his hand seemed far away.

“Close your eyes, Junie.”

She put both palms over them, leaving a gap between her fingers the way she did for hide-and-seek. Usually he let her peek.

“All the way, love.”

The gap closed. He wrapped his hand around the handle. He had thought that deciding would bring some kind of steadiness. It didn’t. He wanted his eye. He wanted to see his daughter with both eyes tomorrow. His teeth were knocking together, and he was desperately ashamed that she might hear.

“I’m still here,” he told her, because it was the only promise he could make and keep. Then he lifted the blade.

When the crowd stopped, Mara kept moving. So did everyone behind her. For a few seconds she was upright without standing, her shoes skimming the pavement, her cheek pressed to the damp wool of a stranger’s coat. Each time she breathed out, the bodies around her took up the space her next breath needed.

The man in the coat turned his head. “Can you get your arm free?”

She tried to say no. She didn’t have enough air for the word.

Then the man went down, and she went sideways over him. For one astonished instant her face was in the clear. She drew a deep, cold breath. A shoe came down on her side before she could let it out. She felt two small cracks in her ribs, distinct as knuckles popping. The shoe lifted almost at once. Whoever it was had been trying to find somewhere to stand.

She could see daylight beneath a metal barrier, six inches from her face. A paper cup rolled through the gap and tipped off the curb. She wanted, with a fierce and perfectly useless envy, to follow it.

When the barrier finally shifted, a hand caught her wrist. Someone else lifted her by the belt. They laid her beyond the curb, where there was room on every side, and a woman knelt beside her without touching her chest. Mara kept taking little sips of air. Part of her still believed that if she breathed all the way out, the space would close again.

Mara heard the key turn and understood, with a clerk’s sort of clarity, that the man on the other side had been given the wrong one. It scraped, stopped, scraped again. She had a few seconds she hadn’t expected to have.

She looked around for something to do with them.

On the desk lay the telegram she’d come to destroy. She had already burned the part that mattered. All that remained was the strip with the date on it, a perfectly ordinary Thursday in March. For some reason she put it in the wastebasket. Then she swallowed the cyanide pill.

She had expected the decision to be the hard part. But her body hadn’t made any decision. It wanted air. Her heart knocked hard beneath her ribs; she drew a breath, then another, and neither seemed to count. She sat down on the floor before her knees could give way.

The right key slid into the lock.

Until then, some small, stupid part of her had been waiting for the next instruction. Get to the station. Change coats. Tell the woman at the flower stall you’ve lost your gloves. There had always been something to do after the thing you’d just done.

Now a man came through the door and shouted for a doctor, and she understood that whatever happened next was his to do.

That was the cold part. Not darkness, not fear. The simple transfer of the room into other hands.

He knelt beside her. His face swam out of focus, but she could see that one of his shirt cuffs had come unbuttoned. He kept pushing it back as he tried to help her. She wanted to tell him to roll up his sleeve. It seemed a pity for such a small difficulty to go on troubling him when it was so easily put right.

By the time she found the words, she could no longer say them.

Nell watched the gray square darken in her palm. “Well,” she said.

Nobody suggested cutting it out. They had all been there for Daniel.

“I want to go while I’m still here,” Nell said. She handed the picture back to Amos. “I need one of you to help me.”

Outside, rain fell through the roof of the abandoned garden center into a row of empty pots. Each pot made a slightly different sound. June had slept there for three months without noticing that.

“We could stay up with you,” Amos said.

“And then?”

He rubbed the photograph with his thumb, as though the marks might come off. “I don’t know.”

“You do,” said Nell, not unkindly.

June was Nell’s younger sister. Everyone kept looking at her, then looking away, which was worse. She wanted somebody else to say no so she could be the reasonable one, the one who understood what Nell was asking. If somebody else said yes, she thought she might hurt them.

Finally Marta spoke. “I can do it. If you’re asking me, Nell.”

“I am.”

“Then I can.”

June heard herself say, “She’s not even sick yet.”

“No,” Marta said.

“We might have all night.”

“We might,” Nell said. “June, look at me.”

June did. Nell’s nose was running. She had always had a running nose when she cried, even when she managed it silently, as she was doing now. June pulled her sleeve over her hand and wiped it for her.

“God,” Nell said, with a small, disgusted laugh. “Get a rag.”

For one second they were sisters in a kitchen and there were clean rags in a drawer.

“I don’t agree,” June said.

“I know.”

“But I’ll stay.”

Nell sagged against her. Until then June hadn’t realized her sister had been holding herself upright by gripping the edge of the bench.

Amos put the photograph facedown. He sat on Nell’s other side. None of them voted. What they had, in the end, was Nell’s request, and Marta’s promise, and the rest of them choosing not to leave the room.

“Wait,” Nell said, and Marta waited.

June expected a message for somebody, or some last instruction about the winter stores. Instead Nell took off her glasses. She folded them and put them into June’s shirt pocket, patting the pocket once to settle them.

“All right,” she said.

June felt the shot in her teeth. Nell’s weight came against her, heavier now, and June held on.

For a while nobody moved. Then Marta laid the gun down and knelt among the spilled potting soil. Amos was crying with his mouth open and no sound coming out. June wanted to tell Nell to look after him. Nell was the one who knew what to do when Amos got like that.

That was when she understood it. Not at the shot. At the small, ordinary job for which she had turned, without thinking, to her sister.

The glasses pressed against her chest. Beyond the broken roof the rain had stopped, but water kept falling from the rafters into the pots, one drop and then another, until each one had finished.

The first time Ruth saw Daniel after she killed him, he was waiting for the kettle to boil. Just his shoulder at the edge of her sight, the washed blue of his shirt. She turned and found her dressing gown on the kitchen door. She took it down, folded it, and put it in a drawer. By then the kettle had clicked off. She drank her tea standing up, pleased to have solved something.

For a few weeks it worked like that. A passenger on a bus had his ear. A bundle of shirts in a shop window had the particular slump of his back. The fright came first, then the ordinary explanation, and in between was a small, shameful rush of gladness. If Daniel was on the number six bus, she hadn’t killed him. She could go home and ring him up and tell him what a terrible thing she’d thought.

Gradually the explanations took longer. She spent an entire lunch break across the street from a man reading a newspaper because she needed him to lower it. When he did, she hated him for being a stranger.

Her sister began bringing groceries. Ruth talked brightly through these visits, telling little stories about work, though she had stopped going. All the while she watched her sister’s eyes. Once they flicked toward the kitchen door and Ruth caught her wrist hard enough to leave four white marks.

“What?” Ruth said.

“The time,” her sister said. The clock was over the door. They both looked up at it, and for the rest of the visit her sister kept her hands in her lap.

That night Ruth tried to remember Daniel as he had been at seventeen, before either of them lived in this flat. He used to peel an orange in one long strip and put it back on the table, arranged to look whole. She could remember being fooled. She could remember his thumbnail stained yellow. But when she tried to see his face, all she got was the shoulder by the kettle. It frightened her that she might lose the real man and be left forever with this scrap. She took the blue dressing gown out of the drawer and hung it up again.

By winter she had learned not to turn her head. Daniel would stay for minutes at a time if she let her eyes rest on something else. She read whole pages without taking in a word. Sometimes she told him small things: the downstairs shop had changed hands; his sister had cut her hair. She never said she was sorry. She was afraid that was what he was waiting for, and that once she said it he would go.

One morning the corner by the kettle was empty. Ruth stood very still. She moved the gown to the other hook. She opened the blind halfway, then lowered it an inch at a time until the kitchen had the gray light of that first morning. Nothing.

Her sister found her there that evening, thirsty and hoarse, repeating the last cruel thing she had said to Daniel while he was alive. It had made him turn back once. She thought if she could only get the tone right, it might make him turn back again.

The first thing Elias did was try to stand up. It made no sense; he knew he was already on land. But somewhere below thought he was eight years old again, in the deep end of the municipal pool, and if he could just get his feet under him he would find the bottom and push off.

His heels struck wood. Nothing else moved.

He needed air. A moment ago there had been room in his head for other things: his name and rank, what he had been told to say if captured, the squeak of a fan somewhere to his left. Now he would have traded all of it for one ordinary breath, the kind he had wasted by the thousands that morning without noticing a single one.

When the water stopped, he coughed until his ribs hurt. His eyes were open. There was a dead moth in the light fixture overhead.

“Which road did the trucks take?”

“Wait,” he said. It came out so softly he doubted the man had heard. He needed a moment to understand the question. He knew what a truck was. He knew what a road was. He couldn't seem to fit the two together.

“Corporal. Which road?”

He tried to picture the convoy leaving the yard. All he could see was Private Bell leaning out of the last cab to toss him half an orange. Elias had fumbled it. The trucks had gone around the corner while he was on his knees in the gravel, reaching under a parked jeep.

“I didn't see.”

A shoe shifted on the concrete. Elias began to choke before the water touched him again.

This time he heard himself calling for his mother, or felt his mouth trying to make the word. She had been dead eleven years. He wasn't thinking of her. It seemed the word had simply been kept somewhere in his body for an emergency, like the red handle behind glass on a train.

Then he could breathe. For several seconds he did nothing else.

In the corridor, a broom scraped across the floor. Three short strokes, a pause, three more. Someone out there was sweeping. The thought undid him. On the other side of that door there was dust dry enough to sweep, and a man pushing it into a little pile before he went home.

“The north road,” Elias whispered.

The interrogator asked if he was sure.

He nodded. He would have nodded at any road on earth.

The rock face stopped her with one hand still reaching for a way through. She had time to feel the grain of the stone through her wet mitten. Then the first wolf caught her calf.

For an instant there was no pain, only the hard, impossible pressure of jaws through wool. Her knee folded. When she landed, snow went down her collar, so cold it took her breath. The pain came as the wolf let go: a deep sting, followed by a rush of warmth inside her trouser leg.

After the long run on numb feet, the warmth was almost a relief. Then it reached her ankle, and she understood what she was feeling. She clapped a mitten over the bite. Blood soaked through to her palm, hot against her skin; on the back of the same hand, where she’d fallen, the snow still clung in a white crust.

The warrant said Nera Voss had stolen nine minutes. On a station that sold sunlight by the hour, this was grand larceny.

Bounty hunter Iona Vale found her in the old dayroom, winding a brass crank beneath a ceiling painted blue. Beyond the glass wall, the night-shift children sat on the floor in their coats. Most had never seen the sun. They watched the ceiling with the grave patience of people who had been promised something by an adult.

“Leave the crank,” Iona said.

“Eight more turns.”

“Nera.”

Nera swung the crank at her. It caught Iona across the knuckles and sent her warrant skidding under a bench. When Nera drew back to swing again, Iona fired her high-voltage stun pistol.

The pulse lasted a moment. Nera’s muscles contracted without her willing them to; her fingers locked around the brass, and her legs went rigid beneath her. Then the pulse ended, her grip gave way, and she fell. The crank kept turning. Its little ratchet clicked in the sudden quiet.

Iona holstered the pistol and knelt. Nera was conscious. Her arms trembled, and for a few breaths she could manage only a thin, strained sound. Iona called a station medic and stayed beside her until she could speak.

“Tell them,” Nera whispered.

“Tell them what?”

“That it’s not supposed to be blue.”

Iona looked up. Beyond the glass, a boy had taken off his coat and folded it neatly in his lap, ready for warmth.

The medic arrived, examined Nera, and helped her sit up. Iona fastened the custody band around her wrist. It chimed to confirm the capture and, after a moment, chimed again to ask whether the stolen property had been recovered.

Iona looked at her bruised hand. She could still bend the fingers. She picked up the crank.

It took eight turns, just as Nera had said. A shutter opened somewhere in the station’s enormous flank, and real sunlight came through the painted ceiling, showing every crack and brushstroke. The first patch landed on an empty square of floor. The children had to get up and go to it.

Later, filing her report, Iona reached the box marked *Property recovered*.

She entered the truth: *No*.

Nina woke because someone was counting down from ten. By the time she got her eyes open, the voice had reached six. She sat up so fast her neck cramped.

At zero, a fluorescent tube came on. Nothing else happened.

That first countdown was just to make her sit up. Somehow that frightened her more.

Her left hand was locked inside a steel box on the table. Across the room stood a green door with a square of wired glass in it. Beside the box, a single yellow button lit up. A voice said, pleasantly, “Press to release. Your hand will be permanently injured.”

Nina waited for the rest. There ought to be an accusation, at least. Some reason this was happening to her in particular. But the speaker clicked off, and she was left with the hum of the tube and the little sounds her shoes made as her knees shook.

She called for help until calling began to feel like a performance for whoever had put her here. Then she called once more, quietly, in case there was somebody on the other side of the door who was frightened too.

What she kept thinking about was peeling an orange. She could feel the curl of rind coming away under her left thumb, the little cold mist of oil. She hadn't known until now that she liked doing that. She would have liked to do it yesterday and pay attention.

She pulled the chair closer and sat. Standing had started to be too much work. With her free hand she tucked her hair behind her ear. It fell forward again. She tucked it back. For a while that was the only decision she could bear to make.

“You can wait,” she told herself.

“Take his irons off,” Captain Vale said. “He’ll walk on his own.”

Ned had meant to say something the crew would remember. All night in the hold he’d been polishing the words. Now, with the plank jutting out over that bright water, all he could manage was, “Can I leave my boots?”

The captain nodded. Ned sat on the deck and tugged them off. His left stocking had a hole at the heel. For some reason he was ashamed of the men seeing it, and put his hand over it until he stood.

Beyond the plank, two sharks circled in the ship’s long shadow. Now and then one crossed into sunlight, and Ned could see the whole animal beneath its fin. One had a crooked tail. He watched it pass under the plank, disappear beneath the hull, and come round again. Until then he’d held on to a small, stupid hope that the fins belonged to something else.

“Captain,” he said.

Vale waited.

Ned looked back at the crew. Yesterday six of them had sworn to stand with him. This morning one was picking tar from his thumbnail. Another was crying quite openly, though he made no move to help.

“I still think we ought to have turned back for Will,” Ned said.

“So do I,” said Vale. “But you drew a pistol on the man at the wheel. Walk.”

The plank was warm under his feet. On the third step it dipped, and he flung his arms wide. A little water splashed up and darkened the toe of his stocking. He wanted his boots back. He wanted the hold, with its stink and its inch of dirty straw. He had been alive down there all night and had spent the whole time wishing it were morning.

The crooked fin came round again.

Ned took the last step with his eyes shut. The boards sprang up behind him. For a long while afterward, the men on deck could hear nothing but the slap of the empty plank against the rail.

The first thing Alice did when the lights went out was put her hand over her coffee, as if the dark might spill some into it.

Then something fell upstairs.

“Dad?”

For eleven years that had been a reasonable thing to call out in this house. She stood beside the kitchen table, embarrassed, waiting for a man who had been dead since February to tell her he was fine.

The man in the dining room heard her. From where he stood in the shadow of the china cabinet, he could see her pale hand moving across the table, finding the coffee again, the roll of packing tape, the empty place where her phone had been. He held a knife. He watched her remember where she'd left the phone.

“Shit,” she said, looking toward the stairs.

She set off with one hand against the wall. The boxes were the trouble. She knew the house in the dark, but she didn't know it with half its contents packed and the other half shifted three feet to the left. Her shin hit something hard. She stumbled into a carton of glasses, caught it against her hip and stood there hugging it until the delicate ringing inside stopped.

From the dining room came one more little clink.

Alice tilted her head. The radiator sometimes made that sound. It was August, though.

Through the fanlight over the front door she could see the yellow squares of the house opposite. Mrs. Vale still had power. Mrs. Vale was probably in her chair with the television on and a digestive biscuit balanced on each knee so the dog couldn't take both at once. The thought was so ordinary and dear that Alice wanted, suddenly, to be over there very badly.

She put the carton down.

A car turned into the street. Its headlights traveled across the hall, up the stripped wallpaper, and into the dining room. For a moment the glass doors of the china cabinet shone. In them Alice saw the reflection of her own legs, the bright brass foot of the table, and a hand at a man's side holding a kitchen knife.

The car straightened out. The room went black again.

Neither of them moved.

Upstairs her phone began to ring. Her sister, surely, wanting to know how far she'd got. The familiar silly tune played all the way through. Alice kept her eyes on the place where the hand had been. She could hear the man breathing now, or else it was her own breath coming back to her off the bare walls.

The phone stopped.

She took one step toward the front door. A floorboard dipped under her heel.

“Please,” the man said.

It frightened her more than if he'd shouted. He sounded close, and quite young, and as though *she* were the one who had done something unexpected.

Alice reached behind her, found the latch and pressed it down. For one awful second the door held. Then her shoulder remembered what her mind had forgotten: it always stuck in damp weather.

She pulled hard and stumbled backward onto the step.

Across the road, Mrs. Vale looked up from her television. For years afterward Alice would remember the time it took the old woman's expression to change—the small social smile, the lifted fingers of one hand, before she understood that Alice in her stocking feet in the middle of the road was not waving hello.

The ration board above the arena showed two numbers: **BELL WARD: 0** and **CANAL WARD: 0**. While the attendants salted the ice, a clerk read the names of the people who would go hungry if their fighter refused.

Mara heard her son's name at number forty-six. There was a pause before the clerk said it. He had reached the bottom of a page.

Across the circle, the Canal fighter was trying to put his glasses in their case with his gloves on. Finally he pulled one glove off with his teeth.

“My wife'll want those,” he told the attendant.

The attendant tucked the case into his coat. Then the bell rang, and both fighters had to pick up their iron bars.

Later, Mara remembered very little of the duel. She remembered getting a mouthful of her own hair. She remembered the man apologizing when they collided, the ordinary little *sorry* of two people trying to pass through a doorway at once.

Near the end he slipped, caught himself, and came at her again. Mara swung. The iron struck his head with a short, flat sound. He fell on his back. One heel scraped the ice, then settled. His glove lay open beside him, palm up, gathering the salt that was still falling from the attendant's bucket.

A medic knelt and touched the man's neck. When she stood, Bell Ward's number changed to **300**. Somewhere under the stands, the bread hatches rattled open.

Mara stayed until the attendant came for the bars.

“He had glasses,” she said.

“I know.”

“Do you know which one she is?”

The attendant looked toward the Canal seats. Most of the people there had started up the stairs. One woman sat waiting, both hands holding a little space open in her lap.

“I do now,” he said.

Mara heard the horn before she saw the little blue car. She swerved. For an instant the woman at its wheel was close enough to touch, her mouth open around a word Mara would never hear. Then the blue car was behind her and the black sedan was still there.

Mara twisted in her seat and fired the pistol back at it. The shot left her deaf in one ear. She had no idea where the bullet went. She'd thought there was nothing but the sedan behind her; now, in the mirror, she could see a whole avenue full of windshields.

She threaded between a delivery van and a taxi. Her heart was hammering so hard that the street seemed to arrive in separate bright pictures: a red light, a paper cup spinning off a hood, a father on the curb catching his daughter by the back of her yellow coat. The girl lost a mitten. Absurdly, Mara wanted to stop and pick it up.

The sedan hit her bumper. Her teeth clicked together. A second ago the speed had felt like something she could use. Now it was carrying her toward a crosswalk where an old man stood halfway across, bewildered by all the horns, still holding up one hand to thank the driver who had stopped for him.

Mara dropped the pistol and put both hands on the wheel.

In the weeks before the sentencing, Nora had wanted one thing: for Daniel Vale to sit in a room with her father and explain why he had left Eli on the road. After the sentencing, when Daniel got probation and her father started setting a place for Eli at Sunday dinner, she wanted something else.

On Thursday night she sabotaged the brakes on Daniel’s car.

She went home and washed her hands with the little bar of soap Eli had stolen from a fancy hotel. He used to bring her things like that. *For your collection*, he’d say, though she had no collection, and now of course she did.

She had worked out why it was fair. Daniel had stood in court and said that anyone could panic. The judge had agreed that a man shouldn’t be measured by the worst minute of his life. Well, Nora thought, let him have another minute. Let him press his foot down and discover what a minute could hold.

If he died, she told herself, it would be because he had driven away that night. Everything since had followed from that. Even what she’d done.

At six the next morning she sat at her kitchen table, holding the phone. Across the alley, Daniel’s kitchen light came on. He stood at the counter in his undershirt, eating a banana. She resented him bitterly for the banana. She had imagined him waking into the last morning of his life with some sense of the occasion.

Then she remembered something she hadn’t thought about since the trial: for eleven minutes after Daniel drove away, Eli had been alive. That was the part she couldn’t forgive. Not the impact. The eleven minutes in which Daniel might still have turned around.

Daniel’s kitchen light went out.

Nora called him. She had learned his number months ago and never once considered what she might say if he answered.

“Hello?”

“Don’t drive,” she said. “I damaged your brakes.”

There was a long silence. “Nora?”

“Yes.”

She heard him put something down. Keys, she thought.

“Are you going to call the police?” he asked.

“Yes.”

After she hung up, she sat for a moment with her thumb over the keypad. She still wanted him to have been afraid. She was glad, in a mean, exact way, that he’d known it was her.

She made the call without waiting to become a better person.

The whistle came before Mara heard anything behind her. A thin, high *zip*, so close to her left ear that she slapped a hand over it, thinking something had stung her. Then came the hard wooden knock ahead. A crossbow bolt stood out of a birch at the height of her cheek, its little vanes still trembling.

She felt her ear. Whole. Warm. For one stupid second she wanted someone to tell her how close that had been. Then she understood there *was* someone who could tell her, somewhere among the trees behind her, and she ran.

It was too dark to see the ground. Sometimes her foot came down sooner than she expected and the shock went through her teeth; sometimes it met nothing, and she pitched forward into branches she could feel but never see. Her own passage made a dreadful racket. She wanted to stop just long enough to listen. She wanted never to hear that sound again.

At last she stumbled into a creek. Cold water filled one boot. She crouched there, both hands pressed into the mud, trying to draw a breath small enough that no one else could hear it.

For a while there was only water slipping over stones. Then, somewhere back among the birches, somebody cleared their throat. An ordinary little sound. Her father used to make it before he read aloud.

Mara got up and ran on with one wet foot, crying now, as quietly as she could.

A rook lands on a boot. The leather gives
a little at the ankle, nothing more.
Another takes the fence post. For a while
the only sound is claws adjusting there.

Beneath a sleeve a beetle finds the shade.
Ants take the long way round a wedding ring.
A fly alights upon an open eye
and rubs its feet. The lid stays where it is.

By noon the rooks have lost their fear of coats.
One tugs a thread until the seam gives way;
one lifts a scrap and flies beyond the hedge.
The empty place it leaves fills up with flies.

At dusk a moth comes down onto a cuff
and opens out two wings the color of straw.
All down the field the hands lie as they fell.
On one of them the moth folds up its wings.

The dog hit Mara behind the knees. She went down on one hip, still clutching the strip of bacon rind she’d found under the butcher shop shelving. Its teeth closed on her mitten. For a second she felt only the tug, as if someone wanted her attention. Then one tooth went through.

She made a noise she hadn’t known she could make. The dog shook its head. Her wrist knocked against the tile, once, twice, and the rind slid out of her fist. They both saw it go.

After five days on boiled nettles, the smell of that little strip of fat had filled her mouth with spit. She’d been saving it until she got home. She had imagined sitting in her chair to eat it, at a table, like a person. Now she was on her belly in broken glass, raking it toward her with her bare hand while the dog scrambled over her back.

Her fingers closed on one end. The dog had the other. Up close she could see the pale grooves around its neck where a collar had once kept the fur flat. Its whole body trembled with the effort of pulling. When the rind tore, they flew apart.

Mara crammed her piece into her mouth. There was grit on it. She chewed anyway, sobbing a little at the taste of salt. Across the aisle the dog swallowed its share in one gulp and stood watching her jaw move.

“Gone,” she told it.

It stayed until she opened her empty hands.

“Can I have my glasses?”

“When we're done.”

“There's a clock right in front of me. I'd like to see it.”

“You don't need to know the time, Ruth. I need the password.”

Ruth squinted. The clock had a white face, and that was all she could make out. “Is it still Tuesday?”

“Yes.”

“Then it's my son's birthday.”

The man glanced at his watch. “Not for much longer.”

She heard a drawer open beside her. Whatever he took out of it was light enough to make no sound when he set it down.

“What was that?”

“Nothing I have to use yet.”

“Put it back, then.”

He didn't. For a while there was only the little electric buzz of the clock. At home she'd had one like it above the stove. You could go years without hearing it, and then one night you'd be standing barefoot in the kitchen and it would be the loudest thing in the house.

“The password,” he said.

“If I tell you, you'll open the file.”

“Yes.”

“There are people in it.”

“I know.”

That was worse, somehow. She'd been saving up the names of those people in her mouth, ready to explain who they were, as if his not knowing were the whole trouble.

He pushed his chair back. Its metal feet squealed on the floor.

“Don't,” she said.

He stopped. She hated the quickness of that word, how it had got out ahead of everything she'd meant to say.

“Have you remembered it?”

“I never said I forgot.”

“No. You didn't.”

“Tell me what time it is.”

He looked up. “One minute past twelve.”

Ruth closed her eyes. She pictured her son asleep with one foot outside the blanket. At least she hadn't missed the party, she thought absurdly. The party had already been over when they'd come for her. She'd been washing blue icing off a plate.

The man came around the table. “Last chance, Ruth. What do you want to tell me?”

She opened her eyes. Up close, without her glasses, she could finally see his face.

“He's nine now,” she said.

Nora tried to call for help. The first syllable came out loud enough to startle her; the second dissolved into a cough. She bent double, one hand on her knee, and sucked in another breath before she could stop herself. It tasted like a mouthful of pennies.

Across the landing, the stairwell glowed orange. Ten minutes ago, in the courtyard below, Felix had looked straight up at her window and struck the match. Even then she’d thought, *He just wants to scare me.* She hated that she’d stood there waiting for him to put it out.

Now the heat stung the backs of her hands. A little clear blister stood up on one knuckle. She stared at it, absurdly frightened of breaking it, until something heavy fell in the stairwell and the landing shook beneath her feet.

The fire escape. Her bedroom. She knew this flat in the dark; she could walk it with a full cup of tea and never spill a drop. But the smoke had erased the far wall, and when she reached for her bedroom door she found the linen cupboard instead.

“No,” she said into the clean, folded towels.

Then she was on her hands and knees, crying so hard she could hardly see the strip of skirting board she followed down the hall. At the bedroom window she got her fingers under the sash and shoved. It rose an inch. Cool air touched her wet face. She shoved again.

A hand slid under the sash from outside and lifted it the rest of the way. Felix crouched on the iron landing. There was soot in his eyebrows.

“Give me your hand,” he said.

Behind her, the bedroom floor began to tilt.

I laid a towel across the hotel desk. It had the name of the establishment stitched into one corner, in gold thread. The management had given some thought to the possibility of a man stealing a towel.

I opened the case. On the lid, in my daughter's handwriting, was a sticker that said FRAGILE. She'd put it there years ago, when she thought I sold cameras. I'd never peeled it off.

The long-range rifle lay in pieces in the gray felt. I took my watch off and set it beside the lamp. Then I put the rifle together. My hands did the work in their old, economical way. They didn't hurry and they didn't pause. When they were finished, I folded the empty towel twice and put it back in the bathroom. Twelve hundred dollars a night and the rail was coming loose from the wall.

I still had six minutes.

The man I'd come to kill was downstairs at a charity dinner, telling a roomful of dentists what their money could do for a sick kid. According to the woman who'd hired me, he'd also had her brother buried under a parking garage. She'd shown me a photograph of the brother. Good face. Crooked front tooth. I'd believed her, which had come as a relief. A man likes an excuse, even one he charges extra for.

I sat on the edge of the bed with the rifle across my knees. From downstairs came a swell of applause. Then it stopped all at once, the way applause does when somebody important raises a hand.

My daughter had called that afternoon to ask how you knew when a peach was ripe. Nineteen years old, living on her own, standing in a grocery store three states away, and for that particular question I was still the man to ask. I'd told her to smell it near the stem. She'd thanked me and hung up. The whole thing had taken forty seconds.

I'd always figured that if she found out what I did, the worst part would be hearing what she called me. Sitting there, I understood the worst part would be the next time she stood in a grocery store and had to ask somebody else.

My watch gave a little chirp. Time.

I let it chirp again.

Across town there was a woman who'd paid me to do a thing the courts wouldn't. Downstairs there was a man who might deserve it. Neither fact got me off the hook. I was the one in the room with the rifle. It embarrassed me how long it had taken to arrive at something that simple.

I put it back in the case. The man downstairs would finish his speech. Tomorrow I'd have to give the woman back her money and tell her why. I wasn't looking forward to hearing what she called me, either.

At the door I remembered my watch. I went back for it, took the little screwdriver off my key ring, and tightened the towel rail while I was there.

It was loose. I could fix it. That was all.

Len did. The paper split on the wet pavement, and four rolls of quarters tumbled out. One rolled in a slow circle until Mara stopped it with her shoe.

She looked at him. “You robbed a laundromat?”

“It’s forty dollars.”

“You owe me six hundred.”

“I know what I owe you.” He kept glancing at the kitchen door halfway down the alley. Inside, somebody was singing along to the radio. “Give me the passports, Mara. My girls are in the car.”

She wanted to believe him about the girls. She wanted him to be lying, too, because the man waiting for that six hundred had her brother’s house keys.

She tucked the envelope inside her coat. Len caught her sleeve. When she tried to shake him off, there was a knife in his other hand. She hadn’t seen him take it out. That frightened her more than the blade itself.

“Let go,” she said.

“You first.”

For a second neither of them understood that she wasn’t holding him.

Rain had lifted the blood off the bricks but not out of the mortar. Detective Mara Venn stood under the butcher shop’s broken awning and watched a thin red thread work its way downhill. At the drain it caught in a clot of hair and cigarette filters.

“Who moved him?”

The patrolman looked at the body. “Nobody.”

“His coat’s dry underneath. Pavement isn’t.”

“Ambulance crew rolled him. Just to check.”

Venn wrote *rolled by ambulance crew*. People had different ideas about what counted as moving a dead man.

He lay on his back between the bins, one arm crooked under him. The left side of his face was swollen past recognition. The right looked ordinary enough: a nick from shaving, a blackhead in the crease of his nose. Rainwater filled the hollow of his ear. From inside the shop came the steady knocking of a refrigeration unit with a bad bearing.

The patrolman kept swallowing. Venn handed him her notebook.

“Hold that. Stay under the awning.”

It gave him somewhere else to look.

She crouched. The alley smelled of wet cardboard, fryer grease and the sweet, dirty smell of a split belly. Part of the man’s shirt had stuck to the wound. Each time a drop struck the cotton, a little more pink seeped through. She left it alone for the examiner.

There was a tooth on the pavement beside his hand. A molar, silver filling still in place. She set a marker beside it and heard the patrolman step into the street to be sick.

One shoe was missing. The exposed sock was pale blue, worn thin at the heel. On the sole, pressed flat against the wool, was a curl of pale wood shaving. Venn looked down the alley. Brick, asphalt, steel doors. Not a patch of bare wood in sight.

“Get a close shot of the sock before anybody bags his feet,” she told the photographer.

He nodded. His flash picked out every drop on the dead man’s face. For an instant the ruined half shone as brightly as the whole.

Back under the awning, the patrolman wiped his mouth on his sleeve and offered her the notebook. “Sorry.”

“Did you throw up inside the tape?”

“No.”

“Then you’re fine.”

Something buzzed against the bricks. The patrolman flinched. It was the dead man’s phone, vibrating in the breast pocket of his coat. Through the wet cloth Venn could make out a rectangle of light, nothing more. It rang until it stopped.

The patrolman looked at her. “Shouldn’t somebody answer that?”

“Not until we know whose voice they’re expecting.”

She checked her watch and wrote down the time.

The client set the remote on the conference table. Behind her, the screen had gone black. The playback counter still showed eleven seconds remaining.

“You said it ended when he died.”

“I said he died at the end,” the producer said.

“What are the eleven seconds?”

“The room.”

“Does anything happen?”

“The light changes. Then the title.”

“I don't want a title.”

The producer opened the approvals copy on his tablet. “You approved *A Man in Winter* on Tuesday.”

“On Tuesday it sounded like a title. Having seen it, I find it sounds like an opinion.”

He struck out the line. “No title. What about the room?”

“Play it.”

He picked up the remote. For eleven seconds they watched a square of sunlight on the wall. It went gray as a cloud passed over. Then the title appeared in small white letters.

“Freeze it,” she said.

He did.

“It's the word *winter*,” she said. “There's nothing in the picture to suggest it's winter.”

“It was February.”

“That's not in the picture.”

“No.”

She turned her copy of the agreement to the signature page. “Keep the room. Lose the title. Is there anything else awaiting my approval?”

“The invoice describes it as a short film. Your office asked for a more specific description.”

“Snuff film is specific.”

“I'll amend it.”

She signed. He made the change and sent the invoice. On the wall behind them, the title remained.

“You can turn that off now,” she said.

He did.

On the ninth morning, Mara found herself breaking the last square of chocolate in half. She had done it before she remembered that Paul was dead. There were his two little rectangles on the silver paper, one for now and one for after supper, the way he liked them.

She ate hers. His she folded up and put in her breast pocket.

By noon, someone had brought a saucer from the galley and set it on the upturned suitcase beside her. There was a small piece of flesh on it, taken from Paul's body. The woman who brought it sat down with her back against the fuselage and began to mend a mitten. Mara was grateful she didn't stay to watch, and then realized that she *had* stayed, and was grateful for that instead.

She had expected hunger to do this for her. There had been nights when she'd woken with her teeth sunk into the knitted collar of her coat. But the sight of the saucer made her feel quite full.

“He'd want you to,” she said under her breath, trying it out.

She had no idea what he'd want. Paul had been her brother for thirty-seven years and she didn't even know whether he'd wanted to be buried or cremated. He was supposed to have told her that when they were old, probably in an annoying email with attachments.

She put the piece in her mouth.

For several seconds she couldn't close her teeth. What she wanted, with the absolute conviction of a little sister, was for Paul to see what a fix she was in and get her out of it. He didn't have to tell her it was all right. He could tell her to spit it out. Either would do.

Across from her, the woman drew the needle through the mitten. The thread snagged; she backed it out and tried again. It came to Mara then that she could sit here until dark waiting for her brother to answer, and the only person who would have to sit through it with her was this tired woman with a hole in her glove.

She bit down. She chewed and swallowed. Nothing in her had agreed to it. That was the break, if there was one: until that moment she'd believed she had to agree.

The woman kept sewing. After a while Mara took the silver packet from her breast pocket and unfolded it.

“Here,” she said, holding out one of Paul's rectangles. “I've got two.”

The first time Arthur opened his museum to the public, a little boy took one look at the woman in the blue dress and said, “She wants to go home.”

“Everyone does, eventually,” Arthur said. He gave the boy a peppermint and turned the sign to CLOSED.

His sister, June, had warned him about children. Adults saw the neat glass eyes, the Sunday clothes, the little card beside each chair, and understood what was expected of them. They admired the workmanship. Children looked at the hands.

June herself was waiting downstairs. He had killed her on Tuesday, after she found the ledger. By Friday he had worked up the courage to stuff her.

He laid her on the long table and set a biscuit tin beside her elbow. In the tin were all the things he had saved from their childhood: a red mitten, their father’s tram tickets, a school photograph with a crescent bitten out of one corner. The bite was June’s. She had been an odd, hungry child.

Arthur took the mitten and pressed it gently against her chest. The wool sank through her blouse as easily as bread sinks into milk. Beneath his palm, her narrow shoulders filled out a little.

That was the secret of his taxidermy. Straw would only give you the shape of a person. For a likeness, you had to stuff them with things they’d loved.

One by one he fed the tickets into her. Her cheeks grew round. A blue marble restored the familiar crook of her left thumb. When he pressed the photograph into her breast, the lines beside her mouth deepened, and there she was at forty-six, looking as though she had just thought of something unkind and funny and was deciding whether to say it.

Only her hands remained wrong. They lay open on the table. June had always kept hers busy, peeling an apple in one long strip or picking dried glue off a bottle. Even asleep she curled her fingers.

At the bottom of the tin lay a little brass key. Arthur recognized it: the key to the pantry where their father used to shut him up. June had stolen it at nine. For years afterward, whenever Arthur heard that key turn, he knew there would be light.

He slipped it into her palm. Her fingers closed.

“There,” he said.

Upstairs, a chair scraped.

Then another.

Arthur stood very still. He had furnished the gallery himself. He knew the sound of the alder rocker, the cane stool, the heavy settle on which the woman in blue had sat for eleven years.

June got off the table. She paid no attention to him. She climbed the cellar stairs in her stocking feet, carrying the key.

By the time Arthur followed, the front door stood open. His collection was making its way down the street in the soft evening rain. Some walked stiffly. The woman in blue had taken off her shoes.

June was the last to leave. At the threshold she glanced back, and for one foolish instant he thought she might take his hand as she had when they were small.

Instead she turned the sign to OPEN.

People were already coming up the path.

The first lash cracked like a wet sheet snapped out over a washing line. For an instant Tomas was back in his mother's yard, ducking under the linen to make her laugh. Then the pain came, and there was no yard, no linen, only the post against his cheek.

“Two,” said the clerk.

He had missed the man saying one. That bothered him absurdly. He wanted the count to be right.

The whip hissed, then struck with a flat, hard clap. Beneath it Tomas heard a smaller sound, a little rip like a stitch giving way. The skin across his shoulder blade had torn. He felt the split pull wider when he drew breath, and a warm trickle ran down his side.

“Three.”

Beyond the post, the kitchen boy stood holding a pail of ashes. He had been on his way across the yard when the gate was shut. At the next crack he flinched so hard that ash spilled over his shoes.

Tomas had meant to keep quiet. It was the one thing he had decided in his cell, and now he could not remember why it had seemed so important. When the lash fell again, he cried out. The clerk went on counting. The boy put down the pail.

After the last stroke, the guard untied his wrists. Tomas slid to his knees. Someone brought water in a tin cup, and he tried to take it, but his fingers wouldn't close.

“Leave it,” the guard said. “He'll manage.”

The boy crouched in the spilled ash and held the cup to Tomas's mouth until he had finished drinking.

The first cricket went down whole. That was a mistake.

It caught just behind Martin’s tongue, a small dry hook of leg, and his throat tried to turn itself inside out. He bent over the steel table, eyes streaming. A string of spit hung from his lip. The cricket landed on the tray again, shiny now.

Above the locked door, the clock changed to **01:42**.

“An empty plate,” the recorded voice reminded him, almost kindly. “That’s all.”

There had to be thirty of them. Roasted, he thought. Tried to think. People ate these at ball games somewhere. Salt and lime. They bought little paper cones of them and complained about the price.

He put three in his mouth and bit down.

The shells gave with a brittle crackle, but the middles were soft. Cold. That was what undid him: his teeth expected everything to break the same way, and instead something yielded like a wet pea. His jaw stopped. Saliva flooded in, thin and sudden, the particular flood that came a second before vomiting.

He gripped the table. Breathed through his nose.

Worse. They smelled like the cupboard under his childhood sink, where a slow leak had dampened the cardboard boxes until their bottoms fell out.

“Don’t,” he whispered, although there was nobody there to listen, not even the voice.

He chewed. Swallowed. Took another pinch.

At **00:51**, a wing stuck to the roof of his mouth. His tongue found its papery edge and worried at it despite everything he could do to leave it alone. Each touch brought a fresh tightening under his chin. Finally he scraped it loose with a fingernail. For one absurd second he stood there wondering where to put it.

Back in his mouth. There wasn’t anywhere else.

The last cricket was the one he’d spat out. A bead of his own saliva still clung beneath its head. He scooped it up without looking directly at it, crushed it between his molars, and swallowed so hard his ears clicked.

**00:06.**

The door opened.

Martin stayed bent over the table. Beyond the doorway was a strip of ordinary hallway carpet, blue with little gold diamonds. He fixed his eyes on one diamond until his throat settled. Then he stepped through.

Somewhere behind him, the recording began again.

“An empty plate. That’s all.”

This time, with his ear beside the speaker, he heard the little intake of breath before the first word. Someone had sat in a quiet room and said that into a microphone. Probably more than once, until they got it right.

Detective Vale found the note in the blue biscuit tin, beneath two baby teeth and a ribbon from a school sports day. It was written on the back of a permission slip. On the front, Mrs. Bell had signed her name to let her daughter visit the aquarium.

On the back, in pencil:

*Dear Mum,*

*I know you will ask why I had to hurt Pip. It wasn't because he was bad. Please don't tell people he was bad. He was the best dog we ever had.*

*He kept sitting outside the cupboard where I put Mr. Lane's watch. Every time you walked past, he'd look at you and then at the door. You always said that was how he asked for things.*

*Yesterday you finally said, “What is it, boy?”*

*So I had to. I waited until after his tea. I didn't want him to think he wasn't getting his tea.*

*Love,*  
*Alice*

There was a postscript, squeezed along the margin.

*His birthday is still the ninth even if we don't have him.*

Vale read that line twice. Then she went downstairs.

Alice sat at the kitchen table in her school clothes. Her mother stood at the sink washing a mug that was already clean. In the passage beyond them, Vale could see the narrow cupboard under the stairs. There were pale scratches at the bottom of the door.

“Did you find my tin?” Alice asked.

Vale pulled out the chair opposite her. “I did.”

“Did you read it?”

“Yes.”

Alice glanced at her mother. “Will you tell her, then? I didn't want to have to say it.”

The tap went off. For a moment the only sound was the little tick of water settling in the pipes.

“I think your mum needs to sit down,” Vale said.

Alice got up at once and drew out a chair. It was such a practiced, considerate gesture that Mrs. Bell almost took it. Then she saw the folded permission slip in Vale's hand.

“Oh, sweetheart,” she said. “We looked for that watch together.”

“I know,” Alice said. “That was a nice afternoon.”

The first piece of skin came off with Nell’s wedding ring. She had been turning it around her finger, as she did whenever she had to make a difficult decision. This time the ring slipped into her palm with a translucent sleeve of skin still inside it. She could see the little whorl of her knuckle in the tissue. Underneath, her finger was gray and quite smooth.

For a week she shed in private. She peeled her face off the pillow each morning and picked scraps of herself from the drain. Her husband, Paul, helped her wash the places she couldn’t reach. He warmed the towels first. Once, drying her back, he began to cry, and she pretended not to hear because she knew he’d rather finish.

The bones went next. She woke to a crack in her left forearm and watched a shallow angle rise beneath the skin, as though someone had pitched a little tent there. Paul fetched a wooden spoon for her to bite. By the time he got back, the broken ends had passed each other and knitted into a longer bone. Her fingertips hung over the edge of the mattress. Over the following month her heels drew up, her knees settled higher, and her jaw broke on one side and then the other. Paul learned to sleep through the small adjustments. The large ones shook the bed.

What frightened Nell most, at first, was how well he cared for her. She made him promise that if she ever hurt him, he would leave. Later she wondered why she’d made him promise a thing like that. Where would he go in the middle of the night? Who would warm the towels?

One evening Paul stood in the kitchen in his coat. His sister was outside with the engine running. He told Nell he needed one night of decent sleep.

She could have stepped aside. A month ago she would have packed him something to eat on the drive. Now she laid one long hand flat against the door and waited until he took his coat off. When his sister knocked, Nell watched Paul’s face. He understood what she wanted him to say.

“I’m all right,” he called. “Go on home.”

After the car pulled away, he went upstairs to turn down the bed. Nell stayed in the kitchen, working her old ring over the tip of her smallest finger. It pleased her that he had known what to do without being told.

*[Five minutes before the scheduled execution. The executioner takes the chair across from Mara.]*

**MARA:** Did she come?

**EXECUTIONER:** Your daughter? I don’t know.

**MARA:** There’s a list.

**EXECUTIONER:** I didn’t look.

**MARA:** Everybody else in this place wants to know who came to see me die, and I get the one man who respects my privacy.

**EXECUTIONER:** I can ask.

**MARA:** No. If she’s here, I’ll spend the whole time trying not to look for her.

**EXECUTIONER:** All right.

**MARA:** If she’s not here, I’ll look anyway.

*[He stays seated. One of his shoes squeaks when he shifts his foot.]*

**MARA:** New?

**EXECUTIONER:** Borrowed. My kitchen flooded this morning. The pair I usually wear was by the back door.

**MARA:** What broke?

**EXECUTIONER:** Something under the sink.

**MARA:** Water still running?

**EXECUTIONER:** I shut it off at the street.

**MARA:** Good. People put a bucket under it and go to work. Then they come home surprised.

**EXECUTIONER:** Were you a plumber?

**MARA:** Had a sink.

*[For a little while neither speaks.]*

**MARA:** I used to cut her hair over it. Sit her up on the counter with her feet in the basin. Only way to get her to hold still was to give her the hand mirror so she could supervise.

**EXECUTIONER:** Your daughter.

**MARA:** June. She came here once with her head shaved. I said, “Who did that to you?” She said, “Nobody does my hair *to* me, Mom.” She was thirty-one. I’d been saving up things to say to her for six months and that’s what came out of my mouth.

**EXECUTIONER:** Did she stay long?

**MARA:** Whole visit. Ate two bags of pretzels. Showed me where she’d missed a spot behind her ear.

*[A light comes on above the door.]*

**MARA:** Is that it?

**EXECUTIONER:** They’re ready. We have another minute.

**MARA:** I had a thing I was going to ask you to tell her.

**EXECUTIONER:** I’m listening.

**MARA:** That I wasn’t scared.

**EXECUTIONER:** Do you want me to tell her that?

**MARA:** No. She’d know I’d asked you to say it. Then she’d have to pretend it helped.

*[She rubs the pale groove on her finger where her ring used to be.]*

**MARA:** At the end of a visit, I always got up first. Even when she was little. My mother would bring her in and I’d get up first so June wouldn’t have to decide when to let go.

**EXECUTIONER:** I can give you the rest of the minute.

**MARA:** I know. I’m taking it.

*[They sit until there’s a knock. Mara gets up first.]*

The first shovelful sounded like rain thrown against a window. For one sleepy instant Ruth thought she was in her old bedroom, with the sash up an inch and the curtains lifting. She tried to sit up. Her forehead struck wood.

The next load came down hard. Among the loose patter was a single sharp tick: a stone.

“Wait,” she called.

It was an absurdly polite word. She had used it that morning when the bus driver started to close the doors.

She raised both hands. Her palms met the lid before her elbows had left her sides. She could feel a ridge in the grain under her left thumb. She pushed until the ridge hurt. Nothing gave. When she tried to turn onto her side for leverage, her shoulder caught against one wall, her hip against the other. She had to lie straight again, as neatly as she'd been put there.

“I'm awake!” she shouted.

The digging stopped.

She waited for the scrape of a shovel taking the dirt *off*. In the quiet she heard air squeaking through her nose. She opened her mouth instead.

Another shovelful hit the lid.

Ruth beat on the wood with the heels of her hands. At first it answered like a door with a room behind it. She knew that sound; anybody on the other side would know what it meant. But the dirt kept coming. Each blow of her hands sounded a little less like knocking, until all she could hear was the slap of skin.

The air was warm now. A breath went in, her chest rose, and then came the awful surprise that she still needed a breath. She took another before she'd finished letting the first one out. The lining brushed her lips. She jerked her head away and found more lining against her cheek.

She wanted to spare enough air to call her daughter's name. Not because Annie was up there. Annie was six miles away at school, probably trying to peel an orange in one piece, a trick she'd been practicing all week. Ruth wanted, for a second, to be in a place where you could call a name and someone would turn around.

Above her, the separate sounds had softened into one low, steady thump. She lay listening for the stone again. Even that small, hard sound would have told her the lid was still close to the world.

There was only the thump, and then the weight of the next one, which she felt through her palms but could no longer hear.

When the factory clock struck six, the fingers of Mara’s left hand opened. She had meant to keep them closed. In her palm was a button from her son’s winter coat, blue with a little white anchor. It fell through the grate beneath the operating chair.

“Personal effects collected,” said the ceiling.

The surgeon had promised her she would feel pressure, not pain. For the first few minutes she believed him. Then something tightened deep inside her forearm, and the pain ran all the way to a back tooth. Her heels beat against the footrest. The surgeon stopped until she could breathe again. He was an old man, with a hearing aid that whistled when he leaned close.

“Please,” she said. “There’s still time.”

“I know,” he said, and went on.

By noon, her spine could receive the factory signal. By one, the muscles along her ribs could count its pulses. Each pulse made her reach, turn, press, release. The first few movements hurt terribly. By the hundredth, they scarcely hurt at all. She found herself grateful for this and began to cry.

Across the aisle, a man was trying to tell a joke. He could only speak during the place in his work cycle when his lungs were his own.

“What did the baker,” he managed.

Reach. Turn. Press. Release.

“What did the baker say.”

His station sped up. Mara waited all afternoon for the rest.

At visiting hour her son stood behind the yellow line in his winter coat. He had fastened it wrong to cover the place where the button belonged. She wanted to kneel and undo it, start him off with the bottom button the way she always did. Her hands went on fitting brass caps to the necks of bottles.

“Does it hurt, Mama?”

She had one breath before the next pulse. She could say *sometimes*. She could say *come closer*. What came out was his name, in the sharp voice she used when he was about to cross a street.

He stepped back. By the time she had breath to tell him she hadn't meant it that way, the attendant had taken his hand.

For the rest of the shift she tried to remember the baker’s joke. She wanted, at least, to be someone who had listened.
