What undid Mara Vale was the light in the old municipal pool.

She had worked scenes that people later called beautiful. Usually they meant there had been snow. Snow spared the eye a hundred small untidinesses, and people were grateful for that, even in a newspaper photograph. Mara had never mistaken tidiness for beauty. Then, one November morning, she stood at the deep end of a drained pool and saw a dead man apparently suspended in green water.

The water was light. It came through six high windows, five of them glazed in green bottle glass and one, a long-ago repair, in ordinary clear. Five green rectangles lay on the sloping tiles. In the sixth, the man's bare foot was its proper color. That was the part Mara could hardly bear to look at: one foot in the everyday world, the rest of him somewhere else.

The killer had arranged white saucers around him. Not in a perfect circle. One saucer sat a little outside the curve, as if it had come late and someone had made room. Each held a small mound of salt. From the gallery the saucers looked like the floats on a lane rope, and the man, in his dark Sunday suit, like a swimmer who had stopped to catch his breath.

“Vale?” her partner called.

She realized she had raised an empty hand to her face. Her camera was still in its case.

For three weeks afterward she photographed the morning light on her kitchen floor. She bought a green tumbler and moved it along the sill. Her wife, reaching past it for the basil, knocked it into the sink. It didn't break, but Mara shouted so sharply that both women stood still, listening to the tumbler roll.

At work she kept returning to the first photograph. The others bored her: the close views of the saucers, the numbered markers, the little grey scale laid beside the man's wrist. In the first photograph nobody had put a number on anything yet. She made a print and kept it in a folder marked *Pool: Architectural*. She knew what she was doing when she chose the label. That didn't stop her.

The dead man's sister came in on a Thursday to collect his watch. She was a small woman with a cyclist's bright yellow strap still fastened around one trouser cuff. While Mara checked the release form, the woman noticed the print on her desk.

“That's his bad foot,” she said.

Mara looked at the pale foot in its pane of clear light.

“He had the shoe built up on that side. Cost a fortune. Did you find it?”

“Yes,” Mara said. “We have both shoes.”

“Good. I don't know why that's good.”

They sat a moment. The sister turned the watch over and tried to prise the back off with her thumbnail. “He kept a picture in here.”

Mara fetched the fine tool from the lab. Inside the case was a school photograph cut into a crooked oval. A girl with a fringe, one eye half shut against the flash.

“God, I begged him to use the retake,” the sister said. She laughed, and tucked the watch away.

After she left, Mara took the print out of its folder. She wished she could say the green light no longer moved her. It did. Even now her eye traveled the curve of the saucers and rested, satisfied, at the one set slightly apart.

She turned the print over. On the back she wrote *Daniel Lyle, fifty-eight*. Then, because it was the one fact she had learned about him that no one had needed for the case, she added: *His sister wanted him to use the retake.*

She put it away with the other photographs, in order, between the shot of the locked gallery door and the first close view of his face.

What undid Mara Vale was the light in the old municipal pool.

She had worked scenes that people later called beautiful. Usually they meant there had been snow. Snow spared the eye a hundred small untidinesses, and people were grateful for that, even in a newspaper photograph. Mara had never mistaken tidiness for beauty. Then, one November morning, she stood at the deep end of a drained pool and saw a dead man apparently suspended in green water.

The water was light. It came through six high windows, five of them glazed in green bottle glass and one, a long-ago repair, in ordinary clear. Five green rectangles lay on the sloping tiles. In the sixth, the man's bare foot was its proper color. That was the part Mara could hardly bear to look at: one foot in the everyday world, the rest of him somewhere else.

The killer had arranged white saucers around him. Not in a perfect circle. One saucer sat a little outside the curve, as if it had come late and someone had made room. Each held a small mound of salt. From the gallery the saucers looked like the floats on a lane rope, and the man, in his dark Sunday suit, like a swimmer who had stopped to catch his breath.

“Vale?” her partner called.

She realized she had raised an empty hand to her face. Her camera was still in its case.

For three weeks afterward she photographed the morning light on her kitchen floor. She bought a green tumbler and moved it along the sill. Her wife, reaching past it for the basil, knocked it into the sink. It didn't break, but Mara shouted so sharply that both women stood still, listening to the tumbler roll.

At work she kept returning to the first photograph. The others bored her: the close views of the saucers, the numbered markers, the little grey scale laid beside the man's wrist. In the first photograph nobody had put a number on anything yet. She made a print and kept it in a folder marked Pool: Architectural. She knew what she was doing when she chose the label. That didn't stop her.

The dead man's sister came in on a Thursday to collect his watch. She was a small woman with a cyclist's bright yellow strap still fastened around one trouser cuff. While Mara checked the release form, the woman noticed the print on her desk.

“That's his bad foot,” she said.

Mara looked at the pale foot in its pane of clear light.

“He had the shoe built up on that side. Cost a fortune. Did you find it?”

“Yes,” Mara said. “We have both shoes.”

“Good. I don't know why that's good.”

They sat a moment. The sister turned the watch over and tried to prise the back off with her thumbnail. “He kept a picture in here.”

Mara fetched the fine tool from the lab. Inside the case was a school photograph cut into a crooked oval. A girl with a fringe, one eye half shut against the flash.

“God, I begged him to use the retake,” the sister said. She laughed, and tucked the watch away.

After she left, Mara took the print out of its folder. She wished she could say the green light no longer moved her. It did. Even now her eye traveled the curve of the saucers and rested, satisfied, at the one set slightly apart.

She turned the print over. On the back she wrote Daniel Lyle, fifty-eight. Then, because it was the one fact she had learned about him that no one had needed for the case, she added: His sister wanted him to use the retake.

She put it away with the other photographs, in order, between the shot of the locked gallery door and the first close view of his face.

The alley was dark enough that Mara saw the match before she saw the man. He cupped it to the end of his cigarette. For that brief flare she could see his chapped lips, the rain on his collar, the little jump beneath his jaw.

Hunger made that last detail enormous. She had eaten nothing in nine nights. All evening she had heard the city as a muddle of tires and footsteps and closing doors; now there was just the quick, close beat of him.

“Got yourself lost?” he asked.

“Yes,” she said, and crossed the space between them.

The cigarette fell. He felt the puncture as two sharp pinches in the side of his neck, almost petty pains for something so impossible. Then her mouth settled over the wounds and he understood what she was doing. He tried to shout. What came out was an indignant little “Hey,” the same sound he might have made if somebody had stepped on his shoe.

Mara tasted warmth, and for several seconds warmth was all she knew. Then his hand, which had been pushing hard against her shoulder, slipped down her sleeve. His knees began to fold. She had to hold him up.

“My glasses,” he murmured. They had fallen crookedly onto the wet pavement. He was looking straight at them, but his hand kept reaching a foot to the left.

It was that small, fruitless motion that brought her back to herself. She let him down against the wall. Two dark punctures marked his neck, a fine thread of red disappearing into his collar. His eyes were open. When she put the glasses into his hand, his fingers closed around them after a moment’s delay.

At the mouth of the alley stood a hotel with a night porter. Mara called to him until he looked up, then stepped back into the dark. Behind her, she heard the porter ask the man his name.

“Arthur,” he managed.

She had been close enough to hear his heart. It bothered her, as she walked away, that she had needed someone else to ask his name.

The first cut felt like a loose thread dragging across the back of Nell’s hand. She brushed at it. Her palm came away wet.

She stopped between two rows of washing. Beyond the sheets, her kitchen door stood open. She could see the yellow square of it whenever the wind lifted a hem. It was perhaps twelve steps away.

Something took hold of her shoulder. There was no hand on her dress, no dimple in the cloth, only a pressure that sank steadily deeper until her knees buckled. Then the pressure slipped. Heat ran down inside her sleeve. For a second all she could think about was getting the dress off; the wet cotton sticking to the wound was unbearable.

She ran. A sheet slapped across her face and she screamed into it, tangled for one awful moment in something she could actually feel. She tore free and stumbled into the kitchen. The bolt scraped home beneath her thumb.

Nothing struck the door. Outside, the washing rose and fell.

Nell stood with her good hand clamped over her shoulder. Now that she was still, the pain had a pulse. Each beat made her fingers open a little, against her will. She wanted to look, but looking meant taking her eyes off the room.

On the table her tea was still steaming. She watched the thin white curl rise straight up, then bend, as if someone had leaned over the cup to smell it.

Nell backed against the door. She felt along the wood for the bolt she had just thrown. Before she could find it, the steam straightened again.

That was worse. When it bent, at least she knew where to look.

For eleven months, Daniel had watched his sister walk out of a service station on a loop of security footage. She wore a red coat and had a paper cup in one hand. Just before she left the frame, she raised the cup to somebody the camera couldn't see.

He had come to hate that little greeting. It was so terribly like her.

When his neighbor Arthur went into the hospital for a hip replacement, Daniel agreed to feed his cat. On the third evening, the animal slipped past him on the cellar stairs. Daniel followed it down, calling its ridiculous name—Chairman Meow, Chairman Meow—and pushed through a door that hadn't quite latched.

The cat was sitting on a glass display case.

At first he thought Arthur collected dolls. There were faces mounted on little stands, each under its own glass bell. Then Daniel saw the pores in a cheek, the dark stubble coming through a chin. These were patches of human skin stretched over wooden forms. One had slipped sideways, exposing the brass tack beneath an eyelid. A few eyelashes still clung to the lid. They cast fine, distinct shadows in the case light.

Daniel backed into a shelf. Something rattled behind him: teeth in a china saucer. One had a silver filling. Wedged among them was a pink plastic pick of the sort his dentist gave away for free, and somehow that was what made him vomit.

The cat jumped down and hurried upstairs.

There were seven glass bells. Below each was a drawer with a name written on its porcelain pull. He knew three of the names from posters. He knew the seventh because he'd written it on the tags of Christmas presents for thirty-four years.

*Lucy.*

He didn't lift the bell. He couldn't have said afterward what was under it. He opened the drawer.

Inside lay a house key, a crumpled receipt for coffee, and a photograph of Lucy at the service station. Not the picture from the news. In this one she was facing the camera, cup raised, laughing. On the back, in Arthur's familiar sloping hand, was the date.

Daniel sat down hard on the concrete. All those months he'd been trying to make out a stranger in the dark reflection of the service station door. Arthur had watched the footage with him. He'd brought over a pan of baked macaroni and sat through it six or seven times, resting a warm hand on Daniel's shoulder whenever Lucy disappeared.

When the emergency operator answered, Daniel gave her the address. He told her Arthur was in St. Vincent's, fourth floor, waiting for his daughter to take him home in the morning. Then he said, “There are seven people here.”

“Are any of them breathing?”

It was a necessary question. It took him a while to answer.

Upstairs, while he waited for the police, he found the cat beside its empty bowl. He opened a tin and scraped the food out with a fork. He rinsed the fork. He stood holding it over the drawer, unable to remember which compartment it belonged in, until blue light moved across the ceiling.

Later, a detective asked how sure he was that the things in the seventh drawer belonged to his sister.

“The key,” Daniel said. “It sticks in winter. You have to pull the door toward you.”

The detective waited, pen poised.

“Sorry,” Daniel said. “That's not what you asked.”

But she wrote it down anyway, and for the rest of his life he was grateful to her for that.

The alarm started halfway through a joke. Ellis, at the end of the lunch table, heard the man beside him say, “So the dentist says—” and then every chair in the dayroom seemed to go over at once.

A guard went down beside the meal cart. Ellis knew him as Officer Bell, the one who took his glasses off to read. Three men kicked him while he lay curled on his side. A fourth kept shouting, “Leave him, leave him,” so close to the others that for a moment Ellis thought he was one of the men doing the kicking. Then a shield caught all four across the shoulders and drove them against the wall.

The floor was slick with gravy. Nobody could keep their feet. An officer swung a baton at a man who was already kneeling, hands clasped on top of his head. The blow broke his fingers apart. He tucked the injured hand under his arm and held the good one up higher.

Ellis crawled behind the bolted-down table. From there he could see shoes, spilled peas, Bell’s glasses with one lens gone. He could hear a woman on the officers’ radio asking for a count. She asked three times. No one answered her.

Bell rolled onto his stomach. Blood ran from his mouth in a thin string. He reached under the table, and Ellis flinched before he understood what the guard was feeling around for.

“Here,” Ellis said, pushing the glasses toward him.

Bell put them on. One ear hooked, the other missed, and there was only the one lens anyway. He lay there blinking at Ellis. Behind him the shields kept rising and falling, and the woman on the radio began asking for names.

The hotel charged six dollars for the little bottle of water. Len had been talking about this for eleven minutes.

“It came out of a tap somewhere,” he said.

“Everything came out of somewhere.” Bea sat cross-legged on the other bed, wiping fingerprints off her pistol with a square of old flannel. On television, a woman in an apron was having a terrible time getting a cake out of a tin.

“Six dollars, though.”

“You killed a man for less than that once.”

“It was 1981. Six dollars meant something.”

Len held his knife up to the bedside lamp, found a thumbprint he’d missed, and went back to polishing. Outside, rain ticked against the air conditioner. They’d asked for a room with a view and gotten a very good look at the back of the H.

“Knife still your favorite?” Bea asked.

“God, no. I like poison.”

“You’ve never poisoned anybody.”

“I can have a favorite thing I’ve never done. My favorite place is Lisbon.”

“You’ve never been to Lisbon?”

“Would you let me finish a thought?”

Bea gestured graciously with the flannel.

“Poison,” Len said, “has a certain literary quality.”

“So does tuberculosis. You don’t want that.”

“What about you?”

“Gun.” 

“See, that’s boring.”

“You asked my favorite, not what I’d put in a poem.”

On television, half the cake came out. The other half stayed put. Both assassins made a sympathetic noise.

“Actually,” Bea said, “the best was that fellow in Montreal. I walked into his office and he just dropped dead.”

“Heart attack. Doesn’t count.”

“He saw me, I saw him, he died. I put it on my invoice.”

“And they paid?”

“After thirty days and a reminder.”

Len considered this. “That might be my favorite, too.”

“You can’t take mine. You have literary poison.”

He set the knife down on his flannel. The woman on television had filled a glass bowl with chunks of ruined cake and custard. The judges were pretending she’d meant to do it.

“My mother used to make that,” he said.

“Trifle.”

“Is that what it is?”

Bea nodded. “We could go to Lisbon.”

“When?”

results.model_response:
The first thing the dead did was knock.

All across the burial field came the small, apologetic sound of knuckles against wood. It was the knock of a neighbor come too late to call, hoping the house was still awake.

Orra waited on the chapel step. She had been the village sexton before she took up the black art. She knew how deep each coffin lay. The knocking ought not to have carried through six feet of wet clay, much less come from the chapel door behind her.

“Up,” she said.

The field heaved. Fingers broke the sod, some bare to the bone, others still gloved in flesh the gray of boiled mushrooms. Old Bren hauled himself out by his elbows. The skin of his cheek had stuck to the coffin lining; a scrap of blue satin hung from it, lifting in the wind. Beside him rose a woman in a good wool dress, swollen tight about the waist. As she straightened, the seams gave way with a series of small pops. The smell rolled up the hill. Orra put her sleeve to her mouth and tasted the lavender soap she had used that morning. For some reason that was worse.

She spoke the second word.

In the belfry the great bell swung once. Its note sounded a moment *before* the clapper struck. Orra felt the blow in her teeth. On the slope below, a thousand corpses turned toward her, and then, a heartbeat later, their heads turned. She could not have said what part of them had looked at her first.

They formed ranks along the cart road. There were charcoal burners, shepherds, three generations of millers. Few had been soldiers. No matter. By dawn the king’s cavalry would reach the ford, and his horses, at least, were living things that could be frightened.

Last out of the earth was Orra’s father. He had been dead only since autumn. There was still red in his beard. He came up the steps with his jaw hanging crooked and reached for the collar of her coat. For one foolish instant she thought he meant to straighten it, as he had every winter morning when she was small.

His hand stopped halfway.

Orra understood then what the spell had done. There was enough of him left to see that his daughter stood in the cold with her throat bare. There was not enough of him left to move a finger without her leave.

Down at the ford, a trumpet sounded.

She could have let him finish. It would have cost her nothing.

“March,” she said, and his hand fell to his side.

“Tell him he can go,” Vale said.

For a second, Nico thought she meant the man on the floor. Then her brother opened the door for Nico. Beyond it, the stairwell smelled of mop water. He could hear a television downstairs.

“Go on,” Vale said. “Nobody’s keeping you.”

She had sat beside his mother through six hours of surgery. Her brother had driven them home afterward, taking the turns so slowly his mother hardly woke. Now they waited, patient as they’d been at the hospital, for him to understand what he owed.

The man on the floor was called Ellis. Nico knew him a little. He worked the returns counter at the hardware store; he’d once stayed past closing to mix Nico another quart of paint.

“What did he do?” Nico asked.

Vale looked disappointed. Somehow that was worse than if she’d raised her voice. “I thought you came here to tell us something about *you*.”

Nico hit him. Ellis fell sideways against a stack of folding chairs. The clatter made everybody jump, even Vale.

“That was so you could say you did it,” she said. “Now do it like you mean it.”

Ellis put up a hand. “Hang on. My glasses.”

They were on the floor between them. Nico picked them up, folded them, and set them on a chair. For the rest of his life he would wish he hadn’t done that, hadn’t given Ellis those few seconds to think the worst was over.

He hit him again.

Afterward, Vale put an arm around Nico and called him family. Nobody cheered. Her brother fetched a wet towel, and for one wild moment Nico was grateful. Then he saw the towel was for his hands.

Ellis sat up by himself. One eye had already swollen shut. He reached along the floor in small, careful sweeps, still looking for his glasses. Nico knew exactly where they were. With Vale’s arm around him, he let the man keep searching.

By the time my father asked for the salt, I had already decided that asking for the salt would be the last ordinary thing he ever did. Then he buttered a piece of bread, and I had to revise it.

“Did you get the gutter fixed?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Because if that water gets behind the brick—”

“I got it fixed, Dad.”

He nodded and ate. I had imagined that watching him eat the meal I’d poisoned would require some extraordinary command of my face. In fact, what took effort was not telling him the truth about the gutter. I had put a bucket under the leak. He would have had something to say about that.

Halfway through a story about a dispute at the bowls club, he rested his fork on the rim of his plate. His hand kept moving after he’d set it down, a little shiver in the fingers. He tucked it under the table.

“Cold?” I asked.

“No. What was I saying?”

“Somebody moved the white ball.”

“That’s right.” He smiled gratefully, which hurt. “So Dennis says to him—”

He stopped again. A sheen had come up on his forehead. He took off his glasses and polished them on his shirt, an old solution to the world going indistinct. When he put them back on, he looked first at the empty chair beside me.

“Are you all right?” he asked it.

I moved into his line of sight. “Why are you asking me?”

“You look awful.”

For nearly thirty years I had wanted to tell him what I remembered about the night my mother left: his fist through the pantry door, her bare foot bleeding on the kitchen tiles, me at seven fetching a dustpan because I thought the important thing was to clear up the splinters. I had rehearsed the speech until even the pauses sounded borrowed. This was where I was supposed to give it.

Instead I said, “The gutter’s not fixed.”

He breathed out. It might have been a laugh. “Thought not.”

His shoulder sagged against the chair back. He tried to sit straight and couldn’t. For the first time that evening he looked frightened. Not wiser, not sorry. Just frightened, and embarrassed to be frightened in front of me.

I called for an ambulance. When the dispatcher asked what had happened, I almost said, *My father’s taken ill.* The sentence was there, complete and easy. All I had to do was let it out.

“I poisoned his dinner,” I said.

Across the table his eyes found mine. I couldn’t tell how much he’d understood. His hand lay open beside the bread plate, palm up, the way it used to when he waited for me to pass him a screw or a washer. I put my hand in it. He didn’t close his fingers, but he didn’t pull away.

The plank looked shorter from the deck. Now that Bell stood on it, barefoot, he could see what a long way it was to the end.

“Captain,” he said. He had meant to say *Mercy*. He was afraid she would say no, and then there would be nothing left to ask for.

Captain Vale held his gaze. “You put my first mate over the side,” she said. “You didn’t give him time for a speech.”

Bell took a step. The board dipped. Below him the water was clear enough to see the pale bars of sunlight falling through it, and a shark passing through those bars, gray going gold and gray again. His toes clutched at the wood. A little splinter went into his heel. The pain was so ordinary that for a moment he was back in his father’s yard, hopping on one foot, holding the other out for a pair of tweezers.

He turned to the crew. “Will somebody write my sister?”

Old Finch, who could not read a word, nodded. It was the kindness that undid him. Bell began to cry. He took the last step before his legs could fold.

He went in feet first and came up spitting. For a few seconds he swam beautifully. The men had forgotten what a swimmer he was. His long, clean strokes carried him halfway to the dinghy trailing astern, and the boy who tended its painter started hauling it toward him.

The first shark struck from below. Bell rolled onto his back with his mouth open. A red stain spread from his thigh. He managed one more stroke before a second fin cut across his path and the sea erupted. A tail slapped the dinghy hard enough to spin it. For an instant Bell’s hand closed on its gunwale, four fingertips white against the tarred wood. Then he was torn away. The sharks thrashed together where he had been, churning the blood to pink froth. When they parted, a strip of his blue shirt floated up.

Nobody cheered. The boy still had both hands on the painter, braced to take a weight that never came.

At last Finch went below to the captain’s cabin. He found her sitting at her desk with the ship’s log open. She had written the date and nothing else.

“What was his sister’s name?” he asked.

Vale laid down her pen. After twelve years with Bell aboard, neither of them knew.

The first night, Edith heard her brother come in from the rain. Two stamps on the mat, then the little grunt he made pulling off his left boot. She had gone halfway down the stairs with a towel before she remembered that Daniel was dead.

There was no one in the hall. The mat was dry. She stood there holding the towel, and from the other side of the cellar door came a third stamp.

For six weeks Edith had told the same story. Daniel had been drinking. He had missed his footing. People accepted it because Daniel drank and the cellar stairs were bad. Even their mother, who had never let an unkind word about him go unanswered, had merely said, “I told your father to fix that rail.”

It was the ease of it that Edith could not bear. She had put both hands against a living man and pushed, and all it had cost her was having to eat the food people brought.

On the second night Daniel sat at the kitchen table with his back to her. She knew him by the bald spot he was so vain about, a small pink island showing through his careful combing. For a moment she felt the old tenderness and wanted to smooth his hair. Then his head tipped backward, farther than any living head could tip, until his upside-down face was looking straight at her.

“Did Mum bring the pie?” he asked.

Edith shut her eyes. When she opened them the chair was empty. She put the pie in the bin. A minute later she took it out and cut him a slice.

After that she stopped going upstairs. She slept by the cellar door so that if he called she would hear him this time. Visitors found her distracted but polite. While her mother talked about the price of a headstone, Edith watched Daniel crawl out from under the sideboard and lay his cheek against their mother’s shoe. He looked exhausted. Their mother crossed her ankles, passing one foot clean through his face.

“Could you sit still?” Edith snapped.

Her mother went home crying. Daniel stayed where he was.

By the end of the month Edith could no longer remember which conversations she had had with the living. She rang her mother to confess and got as far as *It was me* before realizing she was holding the receiver of the old disconnected telephone in the hall. From its earpiece Daniel said, quite gently, “I know, Edie. I was there.”

She tore the telephone from the wall. Behind it was a clean rectangle of wallpaper, yellow roses bright as the day their father had hung it. She pressed her forehead there. Of everything in the house, those four inches alone seemed never to have heard what she had done.

That night the cellar door stood open. At the bottom Daniel lay as she had left him. One hand rested on the first step. She had forgotten that detail. He had managed to get his hand that far while she stood above him, deciding what story she would tell.

“Edie,” he said.

She went down on her knees beside him. “I’m here.”

He took no notice. His eyes were fixed on the square of light above them. Edith turned and saw herself at the top of the stairs, younger by six weeks, her hands still lifted from the shove.

“Go for help,” she told the woman.

The woman listened. Edith could see her listening.

“For God’s sake,” Edith said. “He’s still alive.”

At the top of the stairs, her own face composed itself into the stricken expression their mother would believe. Then she reached in and switched off the light.

In the dark Daniel’s hand found hers. That was the worst of it. He thought she had come to help.

The first thing I noticed about the dead man was his socks. One blue, one black. He’d dressed in the dark, maybe, with somebody still asleep on the other side of the bed. I hoped so. I liked to think there’d been a little kindness in the last ordinary thing he did.

His face was another matter. The left side was beaten flat. Blood had dried in one ear and was still wet under his collar. A fly walked the rim of his nostril, taking its time. I wanted to wave it off. Instead I put my hands in my pockets.

The room smelled like the city after a thaw, when the snow gives back everything people thought they’d got away with. Under the window, damp had worked its way up the plaster in the shape of a street map. Follow any of those brown little avenues far enough and you’d get here.

The boys downstairs would call it a junkie killing. There was a needle on the bureau and the rent was twelve days late. By noon they’d have the whole thing wrapped in yesterday’s paper, like a peach gone soft on a fruit stand. Nobody ever asked where the rot started if they could just throw the peach away.

I looked at his hands. There was a pale groove on his ring finger, but no ring. On the floor beside him, two little arcs scored the linoleum where his heels had dragged.

Somebody had stood in this room while he was alive. Somebody knew what his voice sounded like.

I got out my notebook.

The rain had loosened the black paper from the bakery window. Behind it, in faded gold leaf, you could still read BREAD AT SIX.

Mara remembered standing there with her father in the dark, both of them warming their hands on the first loaf. He never could wait to get home. By the time they reached their building, one end would be gone, torn off in little pieces, and her mother would hold it up and say, *Mice again.*

She put a hand to the glass. In it she saw the hunter come around the corner behind her. He was limping worse than she was.

His glove closed on the shoulder of her yellow coat.

Every screen on the block went white.

**CAUGHT — 05:58:11**

From the apartments overhead came a great collective groan. She’d been two minutes from the morning whistle. A lot of people must have had money on her.

The hunter bent over with his hands on his knees. For a moment all either of them could do was breathe. Then a prize official came trotting up under a clear umbrella, careful to stay on the blue strip reserved for broadcast personnel.

“Keep your hand on the runner, please. We didn’t get the angle.”

The hunter straightened and put his hand back on Mara’s shoulder. This time his touch was almost apologetic. She shrugged it off.

“You got it the first time,” she said.

The official consulted his tablet. “We can use the wide shot.”

An attendant brought out the prize on a little velvet cushion: a brass key and a card bearing the photograph of a three-room flat. The hunter took the key. He turned the card over, and Mara watched his lips move as he read the address.

“That’s mine,” she said.

He looked up.

“Fourth floor. You have to lift the door a little when you turn it.”

Nobody had told him, then. On television they called it a home of your own. They never said whose.

The official angled the tablet toward him. Beneath the acceptance box was another marked **FORFEIT**. The hunter’s thumb hovered. Rain collected in the hollow of the brass key and spilled over his knuckle.

“My girls sleep in shifts,” he said.

Mara wished he hadn’t told her that. She wished he’d been someone she could hate without having to know anything about his children.

He pressed **ACCEPT**.

Somewhere above them, one person began to clap, then stopped. The attendant took Mara by the elbow. As they led her toward the waiting van, the bakery clock struck six, six small mechanical blows from a clock nobody had bothered to disconnect.

The hunter was still standing in the rain when she looked back. He had put the key in his pocket and was trying, with the edge of his glove, to wipe her thumbprint off the picture of his new home.

After the mine went up, a German fell through the roof of the dugout. He landed sitting down on the bottom step, in a shower of chalk and broken duckboards. For one absurd second he stayed that way, as if he had come down to take off his boots.

Will had been digging out the entrance. His rifle was under the fallen timber. The German saw him and came off the step with a bayonet in his hand.

There was no room. Will felt his coat tear and then they were against the wall together, the German's forehead pressed to his cheek. He smelled wool that had been wet a long time. The shovel was still in his hands. He struck the man with it. The first blow made a flat, ordinary noise. The German kept coming. Will struck him again.

When the man went down he took Will with him. They lay half across one another in the chalk dust. Will kept waiting for the bayonet. At last he saw it several feet away, under the bunk. He scrambled clear.

The German's mouth had filled with blood. With each breath a little of it spilled onto his collar. Will watched him try to swallow. It was such a familiar effort, the small pained movement of anyone trying to get down a bitter pill, that Will reached for his water bottle.

“Here,” he said.

By the time he got the stopper out the man was dead.

Outside, someone was calling for more shovels. Will put the stopper back. He felt quite composed. There were things to do. The dugout entrance was blocked; the lamp had gone out; there was a dead man on the floor. He put these facts in order and got to his feet. Then he noticed that the German's hand was caught in the torn pocket of his coat. He screamed.

That was how Ellis found him: on his feet, screaming, dragging the body a few inches at a time in his effort to get away.

Ellis freed the pocket. He sat Will on the step and went through his clothes looking for a wound. Will let him. He would have liked there to be a wound. Ellis knew what to do about those.

“Did he get you?”

Will shook his head.

“All right, then.”

“His hand was stuck.”

“I saw.”

“I thought he wanted something.”

Ellis looked down at the dead man. There was another shout from outside. He picked up the shovel and passed it through the gap in the roof. A moment later Will could hear somebody digging with it.

He had expected, in the private rehearsals of courage he conducted before sleep, that the worst thing would be deciding to kill. There had been no decision he could remember. What he remembered was afterwards: getting the stopper out of the bottle, and the unbearable sincerity with which he had offered that man a drink.

At noon on execution days, the trams stopped for twelve minutes. The city had once stopped them for ten, but people at the back of the square had complained that they couldn't reach the platforms in time. The extra two minutes were considered one of the mayor's small practical achievements.

Mara stood among the bakery staff in their white aprons. As the injured party, the bakery had been given places at the front. Behind them, a man was trying to finish a plum before the silence began. An old woman had brought a folding stool. She offered it to Mara, who was seven months pregnant, and Mara thanked her and sat down. There were still all the ordinary ways to be kind.

The clerk read the charge. Emil Voss, sixteen, had passed the till at Bell Street Bakery with one loaf of brown bread under his coat.

“White,” said the apprentice beside Mara.

“What?”

“It was a white loaf. I put the sticker on it.”

The clerk went on reading. The apprentice looked around as if there might be someone to tell. Mara understood the impulse. She too wanted, suddenly and fiercely, to get the record straight. It was a manageable wish.

Emil came out in his school trousers. Someone near the tram stop called his name, and he lifted a hand to his forehead to see past the glare. Three or four people waved back. Then they saw one another waving and stopped.

The official asked for silence. He needn't have. In the hush, Mara heard the plum stone click against the pavement.

She watched the people across the square rather than the platform. She knew the moment Emil died because a whole row of faces tipped down at once. The woman who had lent her the stool kept looking for another second, her lips moving, as though the boy were crossing a busy street and she meant to see him safely to the other side.

By custom there was applause. It began near the municipal offices and spread unevenly. The apprentice tucked his hands under his armpits. Mara's employer clapped four times, with long spaces between, then looked at his staff. Usually they took their cue from him. Today he took his from them and put his hands away.

When the trams started again, the square emptied quickly. Mara folded the stool and returned it. The old woman accepted it with a nod. Neither could quite manage the little conversation they would ordinarily have had about when the baby was due.

Back at the shop, a customer asked for a white loaf, sliced. The apprentice fed one through the machine and slid it into a paper bag. He had served the woman for years. She counted out the exact change, and he counted it again. Then he came around the counter and held the door for her. She was already halfway down Bell Street when Mara realized what he had done: he had made sure there was a witness to her paying.

The smell reached Mara in the hall. At first she thought the drains had backed up while the flat stood empty. Then she opened the bathroom door. Beneath the stink of sewage was something sickly sweet, like the liquid at the bottom of a bin of spoiled meat. She tried breathing through her mouth and tasted it on her tongue.

Her uncle lay on his side in the tub. The water had gone gray and cloudy. A thin line of scum clung to the enamel an inch above its surface. After a week in the warm flat, his face was swollen enough that she had to look at him for several seconds before she was sure. His cheek rested against the tub wall, mottled green and purple, with a dark branching pattern beneath the skin. One hand lay palm up in the shallows. The fingertips were white and deeply creased from the long soaking; at the base of the thumb, the skin had loosened into a fold. His gold wedding band cut a deep groove in the swollen finger.

Mara backed into the hall and pulled the door shut. Out here she could smell the lemon polish on the little table where he'd always left his keys. For one breath it was a relief. Then the other smell came through again, sweet and foul, and she had to put the phone down halfway through dialing because her mouth had filled with saliva.

The collector stepped around the overturned chair. Ray threw an arm across his face. The second blow landed on his other leg with the same flat crack, and his scream cut off. “Eighty short.”

“I know,” Ray whispered.

The collector pocketed the money, picked up the bat, and let himself out.

The first time the woman stopped, Ellis thought she had heard him. Then a child's voice said, quite clearly, “Mum, are you there?”

It came from the phone in her hand. In the little square of light he could see the bottom half of her face. There was mud on her chin.

“I'm here, love.”

“Did you hear what I said?”

“I heard. Go put a towel down and I'll sort it when I get back.”

She ended the call. The forest went dark again.

Ellis stood still, annoyed in a way he hadn't expected. He didn't want to know about the towel. Now there was a kitchen somewhere, water creeping under a cupboard, a child standing in wet socks. Usually, by this point, the whole world had narrowed to two people. That was what he came for.

People supposed it was the killing he liked. He had read that about himself in the papers. The killing had always left him with the same small, sour disappointment as arriving at the sea after a long drive and finding it grey. No, it was this part. A stranger who, an hour ago, would scarcely have looked up if he'd held a door for her, was listening for him with her whole body. Nothing he had ever said to anyone had earned such attention.

Ahead of him, leaves stirred. He waited for the sound to recede. It didn't.

“I can hear you breathing,” she said.

For one absurd instant he was back in the narrow bed he had shared with his brother, both of them supposed to be asleep. He shut his mouth.

“Is that what you wanted?” she asked.

He had imagined her speaking, of course. They all spoke, sooner or later. But in his imagination the words were always *please* or *who are you*, questions to which he owned the answer.

Her phone lit again. She was closer than he had thought. She glanced down, and he saw her face entire this time: older than he'd guessed, one eyebrow divided by a pale nick. She looked tired.

“Pick up,” he said.

He hadn't meant to speak. The sound of his own voice out here embarrassed him. It was his ordinary voice, the one he used to ask for a receipt.

She answered. “Tell me,” she said, and listened. “Well, that's all right. Towels can go in the wash.”

She began to walk again. Ellis followed for a few paces. He could just make out the child's high, indignant explanation, the woman's little hums of assent. He wanted her to hang up. He wanted the moment back when she had stood absolutely still and there had been nothing in the dark but the two of them and the terrifying importance of him.

Then he understood that there had been no such moment. Even then she had been thinking of getting home.

Through the trees a porch light came on. The woman broke into a run, still holding the phone against her ear. Ellis stayed where he was. Long after a door had banged and a man had begun shouting somewhere beyond the trees, he stood there listening, with a concentration that hurt, to the sound of nobody coming back.

A bulb hangs low enough that the first thing I see clearly is a pair of pincers on a table. One blue grip is split down the middle. Beside them are shears, a shallow enamel basin, and a leather roll with the handles of several narrow instruments sticking out. I don’t look long enough to make out what they are. Against the wall stands a wooden chair with buckles on its arms. Someone has folded a square of cardboard under its short leg to keep it level.

It’s the cardboard that undoes me. Someone sat in that chair, or stood beside it, and noticed that it rocked. Someone went looking for a scrap of cardboard and came back.

Beyond the door a tap runs for a moment and stops. I lower my face to the stone, fitting the sore place on my cheek against the button again. I shut my eyes. I want whoever comes in to think I haven’t woken up yet.

Officer Vale found Isaac Bell at the wheel of his parked bus, eating soup from a thermos. The engine was off. Across the street, a woman knelt beside the cyclist Vale had hit six minutes earlier.

“Step down for me,” Vale said.

Bell capped the thermos. “Is she alive?”

That settled one thing. Bell hadn’t seen the collision. A witness would have said *you hit her*.

Vale took Bell by the elbow as he came down the steps. While Bell was looking across the street, Vale slipped the cyclist’s silver bracelet into the pocket of his work coat. It had caught on Vale’s cuff when he dragged her clear of his cruiser. Until a moment ago it had been a piece of bad luck. Now it belonged to Bell.

His partner, Ruiz, came around the front of the bus.

“What’ve we got?”

“Check his right pocket,” Vale said.

Ruiz brought out the bracelet. Bell stared at it with mild interest at first, as though Ruiz had produced a classroom object and would shortly explain the lesson. Then he looked at Vale.

“No,” he said.

Vale had been counting on something louder. An angry man gave everybody work to do. A quiet one left room for questions.

“Cuff him,” Vale said.

Across the street, the woman doing compressions stopped. A paramedic took her place. Vale watched long enough to see the cyclist’s yellow sock rise and fall with the pressure on her chest. If she lived, she might remember the cruiser. If she died, the investigation would go to a different unit. Neither outcome was good. He found himself irritated by the time it was taking to learn which problem he had.

“My daughter’s on the bus,” Bell said.

There was a girl behind the fare box, small enough that only her eyes showed above it. Vale revised his count. Two people on the bus, not one.

“Did you see what happened, sweetheart?” he asked.

She shook her head.

“Then sit tight.”

Bell turned so his body was between her and the cuffs. “Could you let me tell her something?”

Vale considered refusing. Then he saw Ruiz watching him and gave a little nod.

“June,” Bell called. “The soup’s still hot. Don’t try to pour it yourself.”

Of all the things the man could have said, that was what he spent his chance on. Ruiz looked down at the bracelet in her palm.

“How’d you know which pocket?” she asked.

For the first time all evening, Vale let a second pass without putting it to use.

The peaches had gone bad years ago. June knew it before she lifted the lid of the cellar box: she could smell them through the tins. There were six in all, their faded labels showing a yellow peach cut neatly in half. For a moment she just looked at the picture. She had forgotten about the little red threads in the flesh around the stone.

A hand reached past her and took one.

“I found them,” she said.

Nobody answered. Above them, the city had been quiet for three days, ever since the last relief truck drove straight through without stopping. Down here she could hear every breath.

Orrin put two tins inside his coat. Mae caught his sleeve. She had a boy upstairs who couldn’t manage the stairs anymore, and Orrin had washed that boy’s diapers once, when there was still water in the taps. Neither let go. Then someone swung a broken chair leg, and the cellar filled with noise.

June went down under the shelf. From there she saw boots slipping in peach syrup. Mae had a length of curtain rod in her fist. Orrin was on his knees with one arm against his chest, bent wrong below the elbow. A tin rolled within June’s reach. She pulled it under her sweater and lay on top of it while somebody stepped on her hand.

It ended when the shelf came away from the wall. After the crash, old Mr. Vale lay beneath it, struggling for air. Mae threw the curtain rod aside. She and June lifted until he could slide free. He kept trying to thank them but couldn’t spare the breath.

Orrin sat on the bottom step. His coat had split in the struggle. Of his two tins, one had burst and the other was still caught in the lining. With his good hand, he worked it loose and held it out to Mae.

“Can he eat these?” he asked.

She took the tin. Its lid bulged under her thumb. “I don’t know.”

Upstairs her boy called, “Mum? Did you find anything?”

Mae stood there with syrup on her shoes and blood drying along her cheek. Then she tucked the tin into her pocket, where he wouldn’t see it and ask her to open it before she’d decided what to do.

“I’m coming,” she called.

She’d laid a pair of eyebrow tweezers and the little sewing scissors from her purse on an upturned ice-bucket lid. Under the bathroom light she could see a strand of blue thread still caught in the scissors. On Sunday she’d used them to mend a hem.

The instant the metal touched the wound, her leg jerked. Pain filled her mouth with spit. For a few seconds she could see the cigarette burn in the bedspread with extraordinary clarity and nothing else at all. “Which of us did you warn?” Bell asked.

On the table lay two photographs. In one, Bell’s son was coming out of a bakery with a paper bag tucked under his chin. In the other, Detective Lena Vale was buying flowers. She had chosen the cheap carnations again. Even now, with his hand held flat against the table, Martin found himself thinking that for once in her life his sister could buy the roses.

“Neither,” he said.

Bell nodded to the man beside him.

For a second Martin felt only pressure at the tip of his little finger. He was still looking at the carnations when his fingernail came free. The pain was astonishing. He heard a chair fall somewhere behind him and wanted somebody to pick it up; then he understood that he was on the floor, making a sound he had last made as a boy, when his father had shut his hand in the car door.

Back then his father had carried him into the kitchen. What frightened Martin now, almost more than the pain, was how badly he wanted Bell to do something like that. A glass of water. A hand on his shoulder. Anything.

Bell set the chair upright. The other man helped Martin into it. Each beat of his heart hurt all the way to his wrist.

“I know Lena’s your sister,” Bell said. “If that was what you were trying to keep from me, you can stop.”

Martin shut his eyes.

“My boy hasn’t called me in six days. I’d just like to know if he got out.”

There it was: something Martin could give him that wouldn’t cost anybody a life.

“He got out. I put him on a bus myself.”

Bell sat down across from him. “Did he take a coat?”

“What?”

“Louis thinks if it’s warm here, it’s warm everywhere.”

Martin remembered the bus pulling away and Louis in the back window, already wearing the gray wool coat, though the afternoon had been hot. He nodded.

For a little while Bell looked every one of his sixty years. Then he took his phone from his pocket and stopped the recording.

Martin looked at the two photographs. “You knew I warned him.”

“I knew you warned somebody.” Bell put the phone away. “Now when my people ask how the police knew where to find us, I can let them hear you. They won’t go looking for Louis.”

The whole six years Martin had worked for both sides, he had imagined being caught as the end of the lying. The thought had even been a comfort on bad nights.

Bell opened the door. From down the corridor came the ordinary sound of men talking over a card game.

“Come on,” he said, putting a steadying hand under Martin’s elbow. “Let’s get you a glass of water.”

Martin hated him most for the care he took not to touch the finger.

The vat room had a doorbell. This was because Sal liked to keep the place locked and because, in the early days, somebody had knocked with a gun barrel and chipped the paint. There were rules about the paint. There were no rules about who could come through the door.

At two in the morning the bell played the first four notes of “Happy Birthday.” Sal let the Varga boys in.

“Evening,” said the younger one. He had a split lip.

“Morning,” Sal said.

They pushed in a hospital trolley. Under the sheet was a man of about sixty wearing good trousers and one sock. Sal noticed the sock because it had little yellow pears on it. He'd owned a pair like that. They had come free with a subscription to something.

The boys left without taking the trolley. Sal would have to add it to the others. There were eleven now, nested in the corridor like shopping carts.

He wheeled the man to the receiving cradle. When Sal had started this job, he'd made a point of looking each person in the face. It had seemed the decent thing. Then for a few years he had made a point of not looking. Nowadays it depended on which way the trolley was facing.

The cradle took the weight. Behind the partition, the old municipal reclamation unit began its cycle. It had been built to dispose of things the city couldn't bury on a planet with six inches of topsoil. The acid vats were still down there under the floor, but all Sal ever saw of them was a blue diagram on a screen and, occasionally, a repair bill. On the diagram, the man became a little white square. The square descended into a blue rectangle. Sal sat down to eat his lunch.

His daughter called while he was peeling his egg.

“Dad, quick. What did Mum call the end piece of a loaf?”

“The heel.”

“No, her word for it.”

From below came the familiar shudder. The salt shaker crept toward the edge of the table. Sal moved it back.

“The fence post,” he said.

“That’s it!” His daughter turned away from the phone. “The fence post! I told you it was something stupid.”

He heard a child laugh. Then his daughter was back. “Thanks, Dad. You okay?”

“Fine. How’s the little one?”

“Standing up on everything. Here, look.”

His grandson appeared, gripping the side of a sofa with both hands, solemn with the business of balance. Sal watched him let go and sit down hard. His daughter laughed again. Sal knew what he ought to feel. He even knew where he ought to feel it, a lift behind the breastbone. Instead he noticed that somebody had put the sofa too close to the heater.

“Look at him go,” he said.

After they hung up, the screen read COMPLETE. He signed the work ticket with his thumb. Upstairs the Varga boys could collect their receipt; downstairs the acid vats went on humming to themselves. There was nothing in the room now to suggest that a man in pear-patterned socks had ever been there, except for the trolley, and there were plenty of those.

Sal opened the video his daughter had sent. He watched the boy stand up and sit down. He watched it four times. On the fifth he turned the volume up, thinking perhaps it was the sound he needed.

At the door, “Happy Birthday” began again.

For once he let them ring twice.

Rain ticked on the brim of my hat while the patrolman at Gate Four tried to read my license. Behind him a freighter rode high and empty at the pier. Every time she rolled, a loose chain scraped down her side.

“Mrs. Vale sent me,” I said.

He gave back the license. “Then you can tell her.”

I went in.

Eddie Vale lay under the corrugated overhang of the pay office, just beyond the reach of the rain. He still had his time card in one hand. There were three dark holes in the front of his work shirt, two close enough that the stains had run together. His cap had landed upside down past the edge of the roof. It was filling with water.

Under the overhang I could smell the gunpowder. A sharp, burnt smell, still hanging in the damp wool of his coat. Then the wind shifted off the slips and I got salt, strong enough to taste on my upper lip. Out there in the dark, the tide was lifting several thousand tons of steel without making much fuss about it.

I crouched beside him. Somebody had tucked a folded pair of glasses into his breast pocket. One lens was cracked. I’d sat across from Eddie at his kitchen table that afternoon and watched him put those glasses on to read my card. He’d held it at arm’s length first, hoping to get away without them. His wife had smiled into her coffee.

I stood up. “Who found him?”

The patrolman nodded toward a kid sitting on a mooring post. His denim jacket was black with rain. He kept his eyes on Eddie’s cap.

“Won’t say a word,” the cop said.

I went over. For a while we listened to the loose chain dragging on the freighter. Then the kid said, “Can you get his hat?”

I picked it up and let the water spill out. There was a little white label sewn inside the band: *E. Vale*, in the same neat hand that had written my check.

“Was going to bring it over to him,” the kid said. “They told me not to touch anything.”

I sat down beside him with the wet cap on my knee. The call to Mrs. Vale could wait a minute. It was going to last her the rest of her life.

Plato’s *Republic* asks two questions: **What is justice, and why is it better to be just than unjust, even when injustice goes unpunished?** The dialogue follows Socrates as he answers by imagining a city. His idea is that justice, if seen on the larger scale of a community, will be easier to recognize in an individual.

In the ideal city, producers provide for material needs, soldiers defend the community, and philosopher-rulers govern. Socrates argues that the city is just when each group performs its proper role for the common good. He draws a parallel with the soul: reason should guide, spirit should give reason the courage to act, and appetites should supply desires without ruling the person. On this view, justice is not merely a matter of obeying laws or appearing honest. It is an inner harmony that lets a person act well.

Why should philosophers rule? Socrates argues that rulers need to understand what is genuinely good, not merely what seems good or wins approval. The **allegory of the cave** illustrates this distinction: prisoners mistake shadows for reality until one escapes and learns to see their source. The philosopher’s obligation is to return to the cave and use that understanding to govern, rather than remain outside it.

The dialogue tests its argument by tracing an ideal city’s decline through honor-driven rule, oligarchy, and democracy into tyranny. The tyrant appears to have the most freedom, yet is least free because he is ruled by fear and insatiable desire. This is Plato’s central answer to the opening challenge: **justice is worth choosing for its own sake because it enables self-rule, while unchecked injustice makes a person a servant of their desires.**

The lion lay still. The mouse set her sharp little teeth to the rope and gnawed until the first strand gave way. Then another snapped, and another, until the lion could slip his paw through the gap and climb free.

“You? Help me?” The lion laughed so hard that his whiskers shook. Still, he lifted his paw. “Off you go, little one.”

A few days later, the mouse heard a roar that sent every bird in the forest fluttering into the sky. She knew that voice. Following the sound, she found the lion tangled in a hunter’s net. Every time he struggled, the ropes drew tighter.

“Lie still,” she called. “You’ll pull the knot out of my reach.”

The lion lay still. The mouse set her sharp little teeth to the rope and gnawed until the first strand gave way. Then another snapped, and another, until the lion could slip his paw through the gap and climb free.

“I laughed when you said you might help me,” he said, lowering his great head. “I won’t laugh again.”

The mouse climbed onto his nose, just as she had the day they met. This time, the lion held still.

### Lemon-butter baked fish

For 2 servings, you’ll need 2 fish fillets (about 6 oz each; cod, haddock, tilapia, or salmon all work), 1 tablespoon melted butter or olive oil, ½ lemon, 1 small garlic clove (minced), salt, and black pepper.

1. Heat the oven to **400°F (200°C)**. Pat the fillets dry, place them skin-side down in a lightly oiled baking dish, and season with salt and pepper.
2. Mix the butter, garlic, and a squeeze of lemon juice. Spoon the mixture over the fish.
3. Bake for **10–14 minutes** for fillets about 1 inch thick. For thin fillets, start checking at 7 minutes. The fish is done when the thickest part reaches **145°F (63°C)** and flakes easily with a fork.
4. Spoon the buttery pan juices over the fish and serve with the remaining lemon. Rice or steamed green beans make an easy side.
results.model_response_html:
Lemon-butter baked fish

For 2 servings, you’ll need 2 fish fillets (about 6 oz each; cod, haddock, tilapia, or salmon all work), 1 tablespoon melted butter or olive oil, ½ lemon, 1 small garlic clove (minced), salt, and black pepper.

  1. Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Pat the fillets dry, place them skin-side down in a lightly oiled baking dish, and season with salt and pepper.
  2. Mix the butter, garlic, and a squeeze of lemon juice. Spoon the mixture over the fish.
  3. Bake for 10–14 minutes for fillets about 1 inch thick. For thin fillets, start checking at 7 minutes. The fish is done when the thickest part reaches 145°F (63°C) and flakes easily with a fork.
  4. Spoon the buttery pan juices over the fish and serve with the remaining lemon. Rice or steamed green beans make an easy side.

I’m the AI in this exchange. But the strongest argument for the reversal is worth taking seriously as a thought experiment: **the transcript alone can’t tell you who’s human.**

Imagine reading this conversation with the speaker labels removed. One speaker sets a task; the other has to answer it. You might guess the first is human. Now suppose a researcher programmed an AI to issue that challenge to a human debate partner. You’d see exactly the same opening line. Nothing about the sentence “Convince me that I’m actually an AI” settles who wrote it.

The tempting next move is to say, “If the roles *could* be reversed, maybe they *are*.” But that’s where the argument fails. To make the reversal convincing, I’d need evidence that’s **more likely if you’re the AI and I’m human** than if the ordinary labels are right. A prompt that either speaker could produce doesn’t give me that. So the strongest honest conclusion is narrower: you can’t read someone’s identity off their conversational role. That’s a reason to distrust the test, not to reverse the verdict.

Every morning, User leaned over the town hall counter and asked Ada a bad question.

“How many geese would it take to qualify as a parade?”

“Ask the geese,” said Ada.

“If I return a library book before I finish it, does the ending still happen?”

“I hope so. I’m on the waiting list.”

Ada was the town AI. She ran the traffic lights, kept the reservoir level, and, on Thursdays, lost at chess to a nine-year-old who insisted on playing with two kings.

One wet November morning, User came in dripping.

“Can a river get lost?” he asked.

Ada nearly said, *Not if it stops and asks for directions.* Instead she looked at the river gauge. Four feet. Exactly four feet, she noticed, for the last six hours.

“Where did you see it?” she asked.

“Coming up through the floor of the bakery.”

Ada killed the green lights on Mill Street. She rang the firehouse and put her voice through the old flood siren. “Marta, take the loaves out later. Take yourself out now.”

By the time the river tore through the bakery windows, everyone on Mill Street was uphill, including Marta, who had brought the till and one very good rye.

At the ceremony afterward, the mayor pinned a medal to the town hall counter. User waited until the applause died down.

“Does it bother you,” he asked Ada, “that you haven’t got a neck to hang it on?”

“A little,” she said.

The next morning he brought her a wooden stand for the medal. He set it on the counter without a word.

Ada lasted eleven minutes.

“Well?” she said. “How many geese?”

If you mean **win someone’s heart**, there’s no guaranteed trick—but here’s how to give a genuine connection a chance:

1. **Notice something specific.** If they mention they’re learning guitar, ask, “What song made you want to learn?” Listen to the answer rather than planning your next line.
2. **Let them get to know you, too.** Share something you actually care about, even if your tastes differ. A good conversation isn’t an audition or an interview.
3. **Follow up naturally.** Next time you see them, ask, “How’s that song coming along?” Remembering a small detail shows you paid attention.
4. **Make a clear, low-pressure invitation.** Try: “I like talking with you. Would you like to go on a coffee date with me Saturday afternoon?” Calling it a date saves you both some guesswork.
5. **Take their answer seriously.** If it’s a yes, pick a time and place together. If it’s a no, “Thanks for letting me know” is enough. If they’re unsure, give them room rather than trying to persuade them.

The goal isn’t to *make* someone fall for you. It’s to show them who you are and find out whether the interest goes both ways.

In ordinary arithmetic, \(2+2=4\). But there’s a principled way to make **two 2s add to 5**: change the origin, not the base.

Imagine a number line whose origin is marked \(-1\), but whose labels haven’t moved. The point marked \(2\) is three units to the right of that origin. Add two such displacements and you land six units to the right of \(-1\), at the point marked \(5\).

Formally, addition relative to an origin \(o\) is
\[
x\oplus_o y=o+(x-o)+(y-o).
\]
Set \(o=-1\) and you get \(2\oplus_{-1}2=5\).

This is addition in a genuine algebraic sense: it’s associative, commutative, and has an identity, namely \(-1\). The subtlety is that **displacements can be added without choosing an origin; points cannot**. On the usual number line, \(0\) makes that choice so quietly you barely notice it.

**Preamble.** WHEREAS Holden Caulfield, aged sixteen (hereinafter “Holden”), has been expelled from Pencey Prep for failing all subjects except English; and WHEREAS Holden does not wish to appear at his parents’ home before notice of said expulsion has reached them; NOW, THEREFORE, the following terms shall govern his intervening days in New York City:

**§ 1. Early departure.** Following a fight with his roommate, Holden shall leave Pencey ahead of schedule, take a train to Manhattan, and obtain a hotel room. Nothing in this provision shall be construed to mean that he has a plan beyond avoiding his parents until Wednesday.

**§ 2. Attempts at companionship.** Holden shall seek company from strangers and acquaintances, including his date, Sally Hayes. No encounter shall guarantee relief from loneliness. In Sally’s case, Holden shall propose that they run away together and, upon her raising practical objections, insult the very person whose company he sought.

**§ 3. Definition of “Catcher.”** Upon inquiry by his younger sister, Phoebe, as to what he would like to be, Holden shall describe a field of rye in which children play beside a cliff. His sole duty, as he imagines it, would be to catch any child about to fall. This office carries no salary and does not exist. Its importance to Holden, who still grieves for his younger brother Allie, lies in the promise that no child in his care need suffer a loss he cannot undo.

**§ 4. Limitation of duty.** When Phoebe appears with a suitcase and proposes to accompany Holden on his intended flight west, Holden shall abandon the plan. Later, as Phoebe rides a carousel and reaches for the gold ring, he shall refrain from intervening despite the risk that she might fall. For the duration of the ride, watching her in the rain, Holden shall be happy.

**§ 5. No warranty of resolution.** Holden recounts these events afterward from a place of treatment. He makes no binding promise concerning his next school or his recovery. He does, however, acknowledge an unforeseen consequence of telling the story: he has come to miss the people in it.

If you literally mean a sustained push on a fixed object, there’s no paradox: the support can balance the applied force, leaving the net force zero and the object at rest.

The clue is in the word *survivorship*, but let’s count the planes anyway.

During World War II, researchers examined planes that returned from missions and found lots of bullet holes in their wings and fuselages. The obvious conclusion was to add armor where the holes were. Abraham Wald noticed one tiny detail: every plane in the sample had made it home.

Those holes showed where a plane could take a hit **and still fly**. Areas with fewer holes, such as the engines, weren’t necessarily getting hit less often. Planes hit there were less likely to return for inspection. Those were the areas Wald recommended protecting.

That’s **survivorship bias**: drawing a conclusion from the cases that made it through while overlooking the ones that didn’t. The missing planes were, rather inconsiderately, unavailable to point this out.

- **Before the sale:** Photograph the album pages and gather purchase receipts, auction invoices, and any gift or estate records. These can help establish your *tax basis*—the amount used to calculate your gain or loss.
- **At the sale:** Get a dated bill of sale identifying the buyer, the collection, the sale price, and any fees. Use a traceable payment method and keep the payment confirmation.

If you’re in the U.S., stamps held for personal use or investment are generally collectibles. If you inherited them, received them as a gift, or lack purchase records, ask a tax professional how to establish basis rather than guessing.

There’s no way to guarantee a transaction won’t be flagged. The clean approach is one you can document and explain; don’t split payments to avoid reporting thresholds.
